speechtext:
It miust be quite apparent
to hon. members who are favourable to the public ownership of railways in Canada that not only is the Government attempting to embark upon the policy of public ownership within the limits of Canada, but it is going into the United States. The minister has made a statement as regards the Central Vermont railway. In the memoranda presented to Parliament relating to the acquisition of the Grand Trunk, at page 51, there is outlined a number of obligations that Canada will be responsible for in addition to the debt of the Grand Trunk. There are certain guarantees given-by the Grand Trunk. The Grand Trunk has endorsed certain notes for which it is to be responsible. If we take over the property the people of Canada become responsible for these guarantees. Later on I hope to draw the attention of Parliament and of the country to the guarantee as it affects the Grand Trunk Pacific, but for the moment I wrish to deal with the Central Vermont railway. This statement with reference to the Central Vermont shows that:
The Grand Trunk railway guarantee the interest on the bonds by traffic contract up to an amount equal to 30 per cent of the gross receipts from interchange business.
So that we guarantee these bonds of the Central Vermont railway. In that connection it is interesting to see how far this railway in a foreign country will be able to carry itself, how far it will be able to pay the bonds, and to see how the people of Canada will be called upon to -make up the difference represented by the loss of traffic in connection with a railway operating in a foreign country. We have a statement of the Central Vermont railway business from 1910 to 1917 and in those years the statement shows a gross deficit of $423,782. In certain years it shows a surplus of $325,412, which leaves a net deficit for the seven and a half years' operation of $98,370, or an average annual deficit of $11,809. This is the undertaking that the Government is asking the people to embark in.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend is referring to the statement at page 54, is he?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The facts are as set out in the statement; but the American con-

nections west to Chicago and east to Portland are amongst the most valuable assets of the Grand Trunk railway. My understanding of the situation is that the net profits of the Grand Trunk, by reason of its American connections, are very much larger than the operating deficit which it has had to pay in certain years. The figures which have been given of the earnings of the Grand 'Trunk are the earnings after all of these deficits have been paid and provided for. A very substantial amount of traffic originates on these American lines. The Grand Trunk system in Canada has the benefit of the haul, and the net result is that the American connections are very valuable to the Grand Trunk as a whole and are so considered by the Grand Trunk and by those who understand the railway situation. The Grand Trunk makes much more out' of the haul of this freight than any shortage there may be on the operation ol these roads.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: The fact remains that the people of Canada will be compelled to make up this deficit in the traffic earnings of the Central Vermont. The minister can make any explanation he chooses.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, the people will not be, for this reason: The traffic which origi-.
[DOT]	nates on these American connections, being the traffic that originates in Chicago and the West and which is destined for American ports and goes to Portland, has a haul through Canada of which the Grand Trunk operating in Canada gets its pro Tata.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: Is the minister arguing that traffic through Portland goes over the Central Vermont?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No; I refer to the traffic that goes east on these railways. I may say to my hon. friend that \I am not familiar with the lines on the ground, and 1 am only speaking of the general situation
. as I am advised. The traffic originating in the United States passes over the Grand Trunk lines in Canada, and in a substantial measure, I understand, reaches the Atlantic ports over Grand Trunk connections. The result is that the Grand Trunk system in Canada gets the benefit of this haul of freight which very sub-
[DOT] stantially adds to the earnings of the Grand Trunk in Canada, because my hon. friend will realize that if you increase the volume of the traffic which you are able to handle upon your road you increase your percentage of profits. Your overhead is the same and your cost of

operation must .be maintained up to a certain standard. I! you can increase the amount of freight you haul you add to the net profits. The Grand Trunk in Canada profits not only to the amount of the deficit, if any, which it has to make good, but as a result of this business it gets a very substantial sum in addition, which it adds to the profits of the railway in Canada. If the people of Canada owned the Grand Trunk, instead of their being called upon to make good a deficit on the American lines, having these American connections would so add to the earnings of the Grand Trunk in Canada that there would be a surplus out of which could be paid the loss, if any, in the operation of these connections.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: The argument of the President of the Privy Council is that to wipe out these deficits that have existed in the traffic operation for the past seven and a half years the policy of the Government would be to divert more business to United States and away from Canadian ports.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No; I did not make any such statement. I stated the result up to date according to the information I have Teceived from the Grand Trunk officials who are responsible for the operation of the road and from the men who are responsible for handling the accounts and the business. The result is that they have received more out of the handling of this freight through Canada than is sufficient to provide for the deficit; in fact, so much more that it adds very substantially to the earnings of the Grand Trunk in Canada.
Did I understand the minister to s-ay that this $8,000,000 obligation of the Central Vermont is not regarded as an asset?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, I did not say that at all; I said just the contrary.
How do you figure it? We are to own the Grand Trunk and we propose to purchase the Central Vermont. How do you propose to get the money from the Central Vermont, or how do they propose to get it?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We are not purchasing the two companies, we are purchasing the stock of the Grand Trunk. The Grand Trunk controls the Central Vermont and by getting control of the former we secure control of the latter. The Central Vermont has its assets out of which the claim could be realized if that was desired.
Where would the Central Vermont, under this arrangement get the money to pay this $8,000,000 to the Grand Trunk?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They could issue bonds against the road for that amount.

Then would that show a liability in addition to the $448,000,000 you spoke of as representing the present liability?
Mr. Rowell:	It would be a liability
against the Central Vermont.

When the Central Vermont has not been able to carry itself for the last seven and a half years, but comes out with a deficit, how is it ever expected that the company will ever be able to pay interest?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My information is that the Central Vermont has paid interest on all these outstanding obligations, including the interest on this loan from the Grand Trunk, and that the deficit is after all these obligations have been paid.
Where did the $1,639,637, that the Grand Trunk had to send in to the United States to make good the earnings of the road, go to last year?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That would be an adjustment of the accounts between the Grand Trunk and its subsidiary companies, and the money would be earned by the Grand Trunk carrying on its system in Canada the traffic which originated on its lines in the United States. I am speaking from what I am informed by the Grand Trunk officials.

How much of the $14,000,000 which the minister claims to be assets, is made up of similar indebtedness by subsidiary companies to the parent company, that is, indebtedness similar to the $8,000,000 owed by the Central Vermont to the Grand Trunk?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I have already given a list of $43,000,000.
Were those all similar to that $14,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Not all similar.
How much of the $14,000,000 is made up of similar amounts owed by subsidiary companies that the Grand Trunk own?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I have not got the detailed statement now before me, but it will appear in Hansard to-morrow, showing the figures in detail.
It would be very interesting to know the total.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
There were three very large items:	$15,000,000 due by the Grand
Trunk Pacific; $8,000,000 due by the Central Vermont, and $7,000,000 due by the United States Government.
I do not count those as good assets.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The others could be
collected by issuing bonds against the road.
The liabilities of the system we are taking over would be increased by that much.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The interest on these
loans has always been paid.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The interest has been charged up to the companies concerned and they have always paid it.
Nevertheless, it would increase our liabilities if the Government assumed the dontrol of these roads.

I would like to
have an explanation regarding the $7,000,000 due by the United States Administration. Is that the net amount due, or is there any contra account to go against it, and how long has this amount been due?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is a running account in connection with the operation 5 p.m. of-the Grand Trunk lines by the United States Administration plus, as I understand it, a certain amount due with respect to supplies and other commodities taken over by the United States Administration when these roads were taken over.
' Mr. J. H. SINCLAIR: When was that?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: On the date the United States Director General of Railways was appointed. I should think it very likely, that a substantial part of that amount would be liquidated when the roads are returned by delivering to the Grand Trunk supplies of a similar kind, and possibly of equal value, for those taken over. My hon. friend will see that when a railroad system is taken over, certain supplies on hand are also taken over, and when the railway system is handed back there will be certain supplies on hand which will also be handed back. A substantial part of the amount in question, I have no doubt, will be liquidated in that Way.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
In addition to the deficit of the Central Vermont railway, the statement presented to the House also shows a deficit

on the Atlantic and St. Lawrence railroad (Norway branch) amounting to $1,272,496. The Central Vermont railway, in 1917, showed a deficit of $154,729. That is so far as our connections in the eastern part of the Grand Trunk system are concerned. When we turn to the western American subsidiary companies of the Grand Trunk railway-to be found at page 55 of the blue-book-we find a statement of deficits paid by the Grand Trunk railway in the last seven years. According to this, the Detroit, Grand Haven and Milwaukee railway showed a deficit in the seven years of $1,818,999, or an average of a little over a quarter of a million dollars a year-$259,654. That is the proposition the Grand' Trunk are asking the people of Canada to take over. The Grand Trunk Western showed a deficit on the seven years of $2,843,125. This is a road altogether within the United States, and yet this is the proposition which the Government are asking the people of Canada to take over and tax themselves for. The Toledo, Saginaw & Muskegon showed a total deficit of $545,563 in the seven years, or an average of $77,935 a year. The total deficit on these subsidiary companies in the seven years amounted to $5,205,687, or an average of $743,669, almost three-quarters of a million dollars a year, of railways that are within the United States.
Have the Government admitted that they are liable for these deficits during recent years?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
As soon as they become the owners of a road, the Government are liable for all the obligations of the concern, if I understand the situation correctly. Now let me put on record a statement of the business done by these railways. In 1918 the total tonnage done by these roads in the United States1-which may have originated in Portland or Chicago, or points tributory thereto in the adjoining republic- was 5,479,206.
That was the total tonnage carried over this system between points in the United States. The total business originating at United States points was 24,905,484 tons. The minister will have to make some further explanation to satify the people with regard to the deficits in respect of these United States lines.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Where does my hon.
friend get the figure of 5,000,000 odd tons?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
This is information I have
of the business carried by the Grand Trunk. It is from a source which I have every reason to believe to be reliable.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The figure Which I have of the traffic originating in the United States in the year 1918 is approximately 7,000,000 tons, and the gross receipts of the Grand Trunk Railway Company in Canada with respect to that tonnage are something over $16,000,000. That gives a gross return which enables the Grand Trunk Company to pay any deficits, to pay the cost of operation, and to have a substantial surplus to the credit as a result of the operation of these lines. That is why the Grand Trunk so greatly values these American connections. . If they were liabilities instead of assets, why would the Grand Trunk continue them and value them? We are not responsible for the obligations of these subsidiary companies, except in the cases where the Grand Trunk Railway Company has guaranteed their bonds. If it were considered desirable that these companies should be liquidated, that could be done. But that is not the position of these companies; they are considered a very valuable part of the Grand Trunk Railway system.

The Grand Trunk Railway Company has guaranteed interest upon Central Vermont first mortgage four per cent bonds, of which there are $10,732,000 outstanding, to an amount not to exceed thirty per cent of the gross earnings from the interchange of traffic between the two railroads. Of course, the interest varies with the variation in amount of traffic carried; but I would like to know what is the amount of interest that has been paid annually on this account during the last few years.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
This arrangement is
somewhat similar to that which we have in connection with the St. John Valley radway, but in that case the division is forty and sixty per cent. I have not at hand the information which my hon. friend wants; perhaps I shall be able to get it in a few moments.

Did I understand the President of the Council to say that if we assumed the common stock of the Grand Trunk Railway Company we would not be responsible for the obligations of the subsidiary companies?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We are not responsible for the obligations of the subsidiary companies unless we directly assume them. We are making an investment. If the property is worth keeping, we would be foolish not to keep it and to pay the obligations because of the asset we would receive. But
88J
there is a real difference between an investment in a property the benefit of which we consider it desirable to obtain by discharging the obligations against it, and a direct obligation of the Government to discharge the obligations no matter whether the investment is worth anything or not.
Then do I understand that when we assume the common stock, it does not follow that we are going to become owners of the subsidiary companies as well?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We do become owners oi the subsidiary companies in that we become owners of the stock.
Then if we become owners of the subsidiary companies, do we not become liable for their obligations?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, not if the Grand Trunk has not directly guaranteed them. But this is the situation; We own the stock. If the .company's assets are in excess of its liabilities then we would be exceedingly foolish not to discharge the liabilities of that company in order to get the benefit of its assets and its franchises. But if we have not incurred any direct obligations, and if the liabilities exceed the value qf the assets and franchises and we consider the property of no value, there is no reason why we should not give the stock away; we are under no obligation to pay the debts.

Following out the reasoning of the President of the Council, let me put it in another way. We shall not find out whether it will be worth while to hold these subsidiary companies until after the arbitration proceedings have been had ?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.
Then when and how are we to find out?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The whole question of the position of all these subsidiary companies, their assets and liabilities, as well as the position of the Grand Trunk itself, its assets and liabilities, will be gone into thoroughly before the arbitration, because all these questions have a direct bearing on the value of the stock of the Grand Trunk and should all be taken into consideration by the arbitrators in making their award.

Then do I understand that the Government will come back to Parliament for power to purchase the subsidiary companies, if they deem it advisable to purchase them? Well, the minister need not answer that; I understand that there is

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There is in my hon.
friend's summary so much with which I do not agree that I cannot say that it is right.
In what is it wrong?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I cannot recall all that my hon. friend said, but his statement with reference to the whole position is not as I understand it. Let me repeat. The Government is buying under arbitration the stock of the Grand Trunk railway. That gives it control of the subsidiary companies.
Does it give the Government the property?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It gives the Government the stock which controls the property.
We have the statement oi the minister the other day that it gave the Government the property. Surely my hon. friend is not going back on that.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not know whether
my hon. friend does not know the difference between stock ownership and having a. property directly vested in the person.

The minister will not get away with what I know or what I do not know. What I am asking for is a clear statement to be placed before Parliament and the country of what we are going to possess and what obligations we are going to assume. We are trying to get that piecemeal from the Government.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That has been stated so frequently that one statement more will

probably not help my hon. friend if he has not been helped by the statements already made. We purchase the stock of the Grand Trunk Railway Company through this arbitration. That gives us control of the Grand Trunk, it gives us ownership of the Grand Trunk stock, it gives us ownership of the road by ownership of the stock. The Grand Trunk owns the stock of certain subsidiary railway companies. When we acquire the stock of the Grand Trunk we acquire control of the Grand Trunk. The Grand Trunk owns all the others, so that by owning the stock of the Grand Trunk we acquire ownership of the others.
Of the subsidiary companies?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.
That is the point.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The properties of the subsidiary companies will not be vested in the Crown; they will still remain vested in the subsidiary companies just- as the property of the Grand Trunk remains vested in the Grand Trunk. As the subsidiary companies are owned by the Grand Trunk and as we own the Grand Trunk, we own the whole thing, directly or indirectly in that way.
Does the minister say that we shall not be responsible for the debts of the subsidiary companies?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I said that if we had guaranteed or assumed any obligations of the subsidiary companies we would be responsible for them. We are not responsible for those that we do not guarantee or do not assume obligation to pay. But if a road is an asset; if its assets are in excess of its liabilities, we have an investment in the road, and we would, of course, discharge the obligations for the sake of getting the benefit of the assets. That is the situation.

That is just it. The minister says that if the road is profitable we shall assume the road and pay off the liabilities,
. but if the road is not profitable we shall not pay off the liabilities.
- Mr. ROWELL: Then we would lose the road.
The road would then go back, riot into the ownership or the possession of the Grand Trunk railway, but of the .private owners thereof.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It would go to the holders of the bonds, the creditors. If we did not pay the obligations, the creditors would take

the necessary proceedings to acquire title to the property and have it sold, realize upon it, in order to pay the debts.

My last question to the minister is this: Is the Government going to make a careful examination of and have a carefully prepared statement made in regard to the common and preference stock in the same manner as it purposes doing in regard to the stocks and assets of the subsidiary companies, or is it simply going to take the face value of the common stocks and the preference stocks, put that before the arbitrators for arbitration?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Most assuredly a careful investigation will be made. The members of a government that would do anything else would be fit subjects for a lunatic asylum.
I understand the minister to say that wre are facing a condition by which we may possibly lose all of these American roads.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I did not say so.

The minister says that if he finds they are not a paying proposition, he will let them go. That means that each of these respective companies may be put into liquidation and the road sold. That is the condition faced by the Canadian people.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not want my hon.
friend to misquote me. I said that there was power to do that; I did not say that we would do it. I pointed out in answer to the hon. member for Ohateauguay-Hun-tingdon (Mr. Robb) that these roads had been considered most valuable copnections, and on the information I have, it means a very handsome return to the Grand Trunk railway to have these connections. Under those conditions, if, upon investigation, that proves to be the case, it would be suicidal to any government to let them go.
But the minister told me that if, after an examination, the Government found them profitable, they would purchase them, but not otherwise.

What I mean is this, and it is perfectly clear. The minister seems to refuse to commit the Government as to whether or not they are going to take those American lines. They say: We will become responsible for any of the claims against these respective roads only provided that it is a profitable thing for the Government to take them. I am not misquoting the minister when I say that. It
remains for the future to prove whether they will be a paying proposition or not, and the minister says: If it is discovered that the running of these lines does not pay, we will not assume any responsibility. Then comes the alternative of the people in the United States who have bonds and other claims against these respective roads, to put them into the hands of a receiver in the courts of the United States. We are, according to the words of the minister, facing the possibility, at least, of a con.-dition of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No. According to thewords of the minister, we are not facing the possibility because, unless my information is wholly wrong, these roads are valuable assets. Everything indicates that they are valuable assets, and, therefore, any government, or board of railway management that would not continue their operation would be making a great blunder from a transportation standpoint and would' be creating a burden upon the portions of the railway in Canada which they should: not be called upon to -bear.

I hold in my hand a statement handed to me by the Department of Railways showing the earnings of the Grand Trunk railway, and in that statement is an item of $1,639,317, estimated loss on roads in the United States. That is the record we have, and in face of that, the minister is still hopeful that by some wonderful development we are going to make money. Last year the Grand Trunk found they had to send down to the United States $1,639,317, not being interchange of profit as the minister would let us understand, but a loss on those roads. That is the condition.

I do not think the minister wishes to create a wrong impression, but the impression appears to prevail on this side of the House that the Government has the option, of accepting or refusing to take over the roads which are the property of the Grand Trunk in the United States, through -the Grand Trunk owning the stock of these companies. I do not think we have any option. If this proposed purchase of the Grand Trunk system goes through, we will have to take over these roads in the United States whether they-are paying or not. We would acquire the -ownership of these roadis because the Grand; Trunk now controls them through holding; the stock. Is not that correct?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Absolutely.

Further, the minister states 'that the Government does not necessarily accept any liabilities or obligations of the subsidiary roads. Now the point I want to make is this: If these roads are losing money, if they cannot satisfy the bond-iholders by paying the interest or redeeming the bonds as they become due, is it not the case that these roadis may be sold for the benefit of the bondholders? If that happens, will not the Grand "Trunk system, of which we shall be the owners through holding the stock, lose the investment it has in these rold's? I assume the Grand Trunk put actual money into these roads as an investment. Now that investment may become prejudiced in years to come, if it is not now, through want of prosperity on the part of those roads, in which case, the Government of Canada through its ownership of the stock of the Grand Trunk, will lose its investment in these roads. Do we not assume the risk of a loss-I am not objecting to this-proportionate to, the interest we have in these roads in the United States?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Of course. Theoretically, we assume the risk of a loss on the whole transaction. Theoretically, it is conceivable that railways could not be operated at a profit in the United States, but practically the situation is/ this: By acquiring the stock of the Grand Trunk, which owns the stuck in these subsidiary companies, we acquire these companies. Past experience has shown that that stock is a valuable asset for the reasons which I have already given, and it may fairly be assumed that that condition will continue in, the future. My hon. friend must draw a distinction between our legal position, what we may legally do, and what from a business standpoint it would toe advisable for us to do. As to our legal position, take the case of a company whose Bonds or obligations we have not guaranteed-where we have guaranteed, of course,, we are committed- if it is found that the -operation of the road is unprofitable the stockholders may say: "We are not prepared to put up any more money to keep this road running. We will let it pass into the hands of the bondholders and let them realize upon it." Theoretically^ that is the position. Theoretically that is the position with any subsidiary company of the Grand Trunk, where the Grand Trunk has not guaranteed the obligations of that subsidiary company. But it is a wholly different question whether or not as a business proposition that would be a wise thing to do, and

as I have said, judging by past experience and on the information we have it would be a most unwise thing to do. The Grand Trunk should continue these roads in operation.

I think I understand exactly what the minister is driving at. He draws a distinction between a company whose stock we own and one whose bonds we have guaranteed. In the case of a company whose bonds we have guaranteed, it is perfectly true that if the earnings of the roads are not sufficient to take care of the road's liabilities the Grand Trunk will have to make good the amounts which they had guaranteed. They would, however, come into the possession of certain assets. So is not the minister making a distinction without a difference; because in the case of a company whose bonds we have not guaranteed but whose stock we own, if the bondholders foreclose on the road, is it not a fact that we will lose our investment in that road? What is the difference in the final analysis between losing our investment, and having to pay off certain indebtedness and perhaps obtaining possession of a questionable asset? We lose in both cases, do we not?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: Of what?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Of letting the road go to the bondholders.
And losing our investment.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The answer to my hon.
friend's question is this: If it is not worth our continuing to pay the cost of operation, the investment is not worth anything. We are not losing anything because we deliberately decide the investment is not worth keeping. However, I think it is hardly worth while discussing such remote contingencies.

On Friday evening when this Bill was being discussed in Committee, my hon. friend (Mr. Rowell) was good enough to suggest that hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, not having experience in dealing in stocks and bonds were very apt to fall into error in following the discussion. I quite agree there is some danger of an ordinary member falling into error in attempting to follow my hon. friend and the

Minister of Railways in discussing the different liabilities which we are asked to assume by the legislation, before the House.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I did not quite state what my hon. friend has said.

My hon. friend said something very close to that. I will read what he said. Addressing the hon. member (Mr. Mackenzie King), he said:
He Is not, I believe, accustomed to dealing: with stocks and bonds in relation to corporation and finance, or he would clearly understand that the position he is taking is wholly untenable.
I think the fair deduction from those remarks was that if we understood the position he takes in dealing with stocks and bonds and finances generally we would be able to follow his meanderings. I think it is important to this Parliament and to the people of this country to know what liabilities we are assuming in taking over the Orand Trunk Railway system. I think we are entitled to that information in plainer and more direct and understandable language than we have had from the Minister of Railways or my hon. friend (Mr. Rowell) or anybody else who is standing sponsor for this Bill. The Minister of Railways read long columns of figures this afternoon which it was impossible for anybody to follow. We cannot remember all these different lines of railway and the different obligations we are assuming on account of each. Let us suppose, if our imaginations will encompass it, that the treasury of the Dominion of Canada was overflowing with money and we were prepared to pay cash to discharge the obligations we are assuming in taking over this road, but which we will not have to pay for	until the end of thirty years.
Will the minister state definitely now what the amount would be if we were prepared to draw our check to-morrow for the Grand Trunk Railway and the different subsidiary companies, including all the roads which we are taking over under this proposed agreement? Irrespective altogether of the amount that is to be left to arbitration, what is the total amount of the liabilities and obligations we are assuming?	.	'

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I gave an hon. member that information in a statement I submitted this afternoon.
Mr. iOOPP: Give me in round figures exactly what you would have to draw your check for to meet the obligations that you are assuming, apart from the stock which will be left to the arbitrators to consider.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The statement I read this afternoon contained-
Give me the full amount, just the totals.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: On pages 38 and 39 appears the exact amount of the liabilities. I gave a detailed statement, and I cannot put the matter any plainer than I have already done. It is absolutely impossible to make it plainer.

The minister gave one statement in reply to my hon. friend (Mr. Cahill), and the President of the Privy Council, taking the same page of the same document, gave absolutely different figures; I took them down. I would ask either the Minister of Railways or the President of the Privy Council to spend a moment or two in an endeavour to give us the exact figures. I do not care where they get those figures from, but I do want those who are responsible for this measure, which will impose upon the people this gigantic obligation, to state in dollars and cents exactly what the check would be if they had to draw it tomorrow. That is a fair question, and one that can be easily answered.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It cannot be answered.
Why?-I mean apart from what the arbitrators will deal with.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes. I will tell my hon. friend why his question cannot be answered. Take the $60,000,000 of guaranteed stock which we discharge by a four per cent obligation. If I said definitely $60,000,000 it would not be true.
Why?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Because, the position
would be different if we discharged it in cash. Money is worth to-day five and a half per cent, whereas we are able to discharge it by a four per cent obligation. You would have to discount that by a veTy substantial sum; I do not know how much. I do not know what four per cent for a $60,000,000 obligation for thirty years is .worth to-day, nor can any one say exactly what its cash value is. Similarly take the perpetual debentures. I do not know what they are worth to-day having regard to the rate of interest they bear. What we do know is that so far as the debenture stock is concerned, that is an obligation which we can take up after 30 years and on which in the meantime we pay four per cent interest. We can take that up at the end of thirty years or thereafter.

Does the minister say
"debenture stock"?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I meant guaranteed
stock. No one can say to-day what the cash value of that is.
Without reference to the possible discount, can the minister give us the face value?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The face value and the real value may be very different propositions. The face value has been given repeatedly.
Give* us in round numbers.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The face value of the
guaranteed stock is $60,000,000, but that is not what the cash value is by any possible means. That is not the obligation Canada would have to pay in cash.
We have the sixty million dollars; what else?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend will see on page 38 that the funded debt amounts to $155,373,806.20. The second mortgage equipment bonds and certain other bonds, etc., amount to $18,184,738.42. Then there are certain equipment notes and loans, less credits, amounting to $5,344,207.54. Then there are secured and unsecured notes, $35,548,235.08. This last item includes notes unsecured, $3,916,362.18. If my hon. friend adds these totals together, he will have, leaving out the guaranteed stock for the time being, the obligations against the Grand Trunk railway.
What about the $22,000,000 or current liabilities?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Those liabilities are offset by assets vastly in excess. In dealing with the obligations that the road bears you cannot add the current liabilities without taking into account the current assets. Now, my hon. friend has the obligations of the Grand Trunk railway. In addition to that, if he wants the obligations of the Grand Trunk Pacific
I want all the obligations the Government are attempting to take over by this arrangement.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We are taking over only those we absolutely guarantee. My hon. friend uses the phrase, " talcing over." Unfortunately we are already in that position in relation to the Grand Trunk Pacific system. We have had to pay deficits right along on it, or would have had to do so

had we not refused. The total obligations of the Grand Trunk Pacific appear on page '42. Principal amounts to $216,253,111, which includes the branch lines.
Does that include interest up to date?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Government has had' to pay interest until recently. It has not paid interest since the road went into the hands of the receiver.
What they have paid is included in this statement?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes; what the Government has paid is included in the loans advanced to the company.

Do I understand, then, that by adding these items together which the minister has just given we have the total obligation we are assuming by the legislation that is now before this committee, plus whatever sum is allowed by the arbitrators?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I did not say that. These are the obligations of the roads, off-set by corresponding assets. The obligations we assume are those which we directly undertake to assume under the agreement. It is all an investment, and in order to get the benefit of the investment we must take into consideration the assets and liabilities.
To get whatever assets the Grand Trunk Company and the subsidiary companies constitute we are assuming these obligations.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We get the several constituent companies with the obligations resting upon these several constituent companies and we get the assets with them.
I gather from the minister that the par value of the stock that would be arbitrated would be $180,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Approximately so.

Those are the two amounts.
The amount which my hon. friend has just given me and the award that the arbitrators give on the $180,000,000 par value of stock is what this country will pay for the assets we get from the Grand Trunk. Ia that correct?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is not what we are paying for the assets. These are obligations against the assets we are getting. I think my hon. friend should add to that certain liabilities that are against the subsidiary companies in the United States, and amounting to $26,460,965.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Before the
committee rose on Friday evening the President of the Council gave a reason why this measure should be hurried through at the present time. I want to make perfectly sure that I understand his meaning. As I gathered from his words, it was to the effect that if the measure were permitted to stand over for a short time certain influences would be at work between now and the next session of Parliament to prevent the measure going through. Am I right in understanding that to be the tenor of the hon. gentleman's remarks?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend will see what I said if he looks up Hansard. 1 gave a number of reasons why I thought it was in the public interest that this legislation should go on through and one was that I believed that powerful interests opposed to it would utilize any short delay in organizing hostility to it. I have no hesitation in repeating that to-night. I believe the Government to-day is fighting the battle of the people, we are fighting in the public interest, and for the benefit of the whole people of Canada. It is one of the most important battles for the people that has ever been fought in the history of Canada.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I think that what the minister has said is precisely what he said the other evening. He also at the same time made the following statement, which appears at page 1419 of Hansard. Speaking in reply to my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) he said:
My hon. friend has the same right to be opposed to this transaction as I have to be in favour of it. But he will not be any less opposed to it in February next than he is now and my hon. friends opposite will not be any less opposed to it in February next than they are now.
In other words, what the President of the Council has said is that in so far as this side of the House is concerned, it is not likely to change its attitude towards the measure. It necessarily follows that the attitude of Parliament can only be changed because of some change on the part of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. He must see that his remark is a reflection on every member sitting behind him if he leaves it in that form. I want to be quite sure that I know what his meaning is because the powerful corporations to which my hon. friend has referred cannot exert any influence on this side of the House but, according to his own remarks, they can exert influence on hon. gentlemen sitting behind him.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am sure the committee will appreciate my hon. friend's very ingenious application of my remarks.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is very obvious.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I made it quite clear that there would be no change in the men on this side of the House and mly statement says so. I further said, that being so and the men on both sides having evidently reached their conclusion as to what should be done, should we not go on with the Bill?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My hon. friend, if he is not reflecting on the members of his own side, is reflecting on honorable members in general, because it is a reflection to say that the memlbera of Parliament are subject' to the influence of corporations in the matter of this legislation.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My words speak for themselves. I know what I said. I have nothing to withdraw. I have made no reflection upon any hon. member of this House.
Is it correct to say that the total funded debt to be assumed is $448,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I stated that the total funded debt as it appears at pages 40-41, including the Grand Trunk, the Grand Trunk Pacific and the subsidiary lines in the United tSates, bonds, notes, and loans is $448,703,356.
To the liabilities of the Grand Trunk system would be added $35,000,000 of current notes payable?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My understanding is that the amount is in this statement that I have already given.
No.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The moneys advanced by the Dominion Government to the Grand Trunk Pacific because they constitute liabilities of these corporations, are included in these figures.
Where, in the statement will I find notes payable and current liabilities included in this $448,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend will find current liabilities on pages 38 and 39 amounting to $22,801,474.35.
That will be added to the total liabilities of this undertaking?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No; I do not think so; that is offset by current assets. It should not be included in the bonded obligations or obligations by way of loan?

If I owe my hon. friend
some money and tell him I have assets he will not accept that statement; he will want to know that the money will be paid now. Is the liability against the Grand Trunk which appears in this detailed statement at page 38 a liability against this undertaking which we are taking over?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is so stated on this
page.

'There is the $35,000,000
and there' is also the $22,000,000 representing current liabilities which will be liabilities against this undertaking?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, the $35,000,000 or the greater part of it is included in the $448,000,000 but the $22,000,000 is not.
Where would it be in the $448,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I understand it is included in the amount of $202,000,000.
Does the Minister of Railways say it is in the $202,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes, I gave that statement to-day in detail. I gave the figure $266,000,000 which is made up of this $202,000,000 and the $60,000,000 guarantee. Those added together make the $266,000,000 and that is included in the statement.
What was included, the $35,000,000 of stock issued?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The greater part of the $35,000,000 is included in the $448,000,000, but not the $3,916,362 of notes payable-unsecured; nor the current liabilities of $22,801,474, the sum of $3,455,344 of reserves, or the sum of $7,286,995 representing advances to controlled companies, for this reason: The current liabilities are offset by the current assets, and we have assets on the opposite side of the account to balance at least three of these items,
There is a total funded debt of $173,000,000 in round figures, is there not?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes.
And there is an item of $35,000,000 notes, in round figures? What is the total of these, two items?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Two hundred and nine millions.
I would also like to know what total the minister has for the item to be found on page 40, " Grand. Trunk Railway Company funded debt, bonds and debentures. Notes-Loans?"

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has been discussing liabilities taken from the annual statement to December 31, 1917, whereas the statement I gave to-day applied to 1918, and naturally there would be a difference between the two statements.

Before the House rises
for recess I would also like to ask the minister a question so that he can prepare the necessary information in the meantime. It must be quite apparent to the minister and to the committee as well that when we are entering into an undertaking of this kind we should have a statement up to date of the total liabilities that we are to assume under the present Bill and a statement of the total assets so that we may deal intelligently with the subject. It is all very well to say, ''You are going to arbitrate," but before you arbitrate it is necessary to see whether or not there is anything to arbitrate. Before we pass this legislation empowering the Government to pay $60,000,000 to certain shareholders, and before any arbitration is entered into, we ought to know what the liabilities against the undertaking amount to, and also what the assets are.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall clause 2 carry? Mr. CAHILL: No.
At 6 o'clock the committee took recess.
After Kecess.
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Just before six o'clock I had pointed out that the amount of the funded debt was given in the statement of December 31, 1918, as $202,000,000. The minister said that the item of $35,000,000 should be added to the amount of the funded debt as given on page 38 of the statement of December 31, 1918. That would bring the total up to $209,000,000; I would like the minister to explain the discrepancy in these figures.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
In that $35,000,000 there is an item of $3,916,362.18, notes payable unsecured. In reality that should be under ' Current Liabilities " or some other heading. The other three items of $12,000,000, $4,000,000 and $14,000,000 represent money borrowed on notes but secured by debenture stock as collateral; and in respect of these three items my hon. friend will see the following note at the foot of page 39:
$50,126,665.98 of Grand Trunk 4 per cent debenture stock further than above has been

Issued as collateral security for notes indicated thus.
The hon. member asked me a question something like this:	Supposing you had
the money, what would it take to clean up everything? Well, the $205,190,417.52 represents Grand Trunk debenture stock, some at four per cent, some at five per cent, some at six per cent; so that it would be hard to estimate just how much that stock would be worth if you were going to buy it. The same is true of the guaranteed stock, $60,833,332.51. The amount for which the Grand Trunk Railway Company is obligated in respect to guarantees of its subsidiary companies is $18,936,377.29. Adding these various amounts together, you get $284,980,127.32. Then there is the Grand Trunk Pacific and its branch lines, $216.253,111, so that the total liabilities, including the subsidiary companies, the Grand Trunk Pacific and its branch lines, and the lines in the United States, would be $501,233,238. These are figures which I myself have computed; they are subject to correction by my officials. I think, however, that they are fairly close to the mark. I asked the officials the other day to give me a statement of how the accounts stand right up to date. Of course, in most of these amounts there would be very little change-not enough to be of very serious import in this discussion.
Now, I.will sum up these figures in order that hon. members may see how they stand. The funded debt amounts to $205,190,417.52; guaranteed stock $60,833,332.51; guarantees on American lines, $18,936,377.29; total on Grand Trunk and subsidiary companies, irrespective of Grand Trunk Pacific, $284,980,127.32. If you wish to take in the Grand Trunk Pacific and its branch lines, add $216,253,111 to that and you get a total of $501,233,238.
In that amount are included 'moneys advanced by the Government in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific. In addition to that the hon. member will see that there is an amount of notes p-ayable unsecured, $3,916,362.18 which should toe in the current liabilities. If we add that to the item of current liabilities amounting to $22,801,474.35, we have a total for the two items of $20,717,836.53 of current liabilities. But we have on the opposite' side current assets amounting to $51,827,879.16 which would go to meet the current liabilities, so that there are no interest charges, the one item toeing s apposed to offset the other. Then there are two other items, $3,455,344.86 and $7,286,995.75 as shown in the statement, tout if hon. members will look at the other side
of the account, they will find the same amount to balance them up; they are really simple bookkeeping accounts. My officials have not returned, but these figures are pretty nearly accurate. They are, however, subject to correction should my officials find any difference.

I want to go back to the statement again and straighten it -out if that is at all possible. In the Grand Trunk statement on page 40 the total funded debt, etc., is shown as amounting to $202,332,997. On page 39, there is an item of $173,558,544.62, another item of $15,142,633.13 and another item in connection with equipment amounting to $5,344,207.54. These three items would total about $194,000,000. If you add to that the item of $35,548,235.08' less the notes payable unsecured amounting to $3,916,362.18, you get an amount much larger than $202,332,997. I should like the minister to explain the wide discrepancy in those figures.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The item of $173,558,44.62 plus the three items of secured notes, that is, the $12,166,666.50, the' $4,866,666.60 and the $14,598,539.80, make up the amount I have stated, $205,190,417.52. The other item of $5,344,207.54 is equipment notes against the equipment, and the railways always take that as a charge against the cost of operation. The interest on the equipment, and' the deductions each year are taken out of operation and, therefore, that is not included in what we call capital account or what would be charged against the road; it is a liability against the equipment. What is really against the road is comprised in the amounts I have stated, guaranteed stock, funded debt, and so on, amounting to $501,233,238. The other items are liabilities in connection with operation, and there are assets on the opposite side to offset them.

In order to arrive at an intelligent understanding of this matter, it is necessary to know the total liabilities of the undertaking. We can then find out what the assets amount to. It was stated this afternoon that most of this $43,000,000 item consisted- of loans to subsidiary companies that may or may not be of any value to this undertaking. What I want to get at are the total liabilities of the undertaking that the Government is going to take over.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The total liabilities comprise the amounts that I have stated, totalling $501,233,238, a lot of which is stock at a low rate of interest, and the current

liabilities amounting to $26,717,836.53. Then there are advances to American and Canadian lines amounting to about $18,930,377, but as they are subsidiary companies, that is not considered in the capital liabilities against the Grand Trunk Railway system. I do not think I can put the matter plainer than to say that the total liabilities amount to $501,233,238.

Is that the funded debt?
.Mr. J. D. REID: Yes. What you call the guaranteed stock and the funded debt.
Plus the $35,000,000 item.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: All of the $35,000,000 item except the item "notes payable unsecured" amounting to $3,916,362.18 is in- eluded in that amount.
Is the item of $15,000,000, advanced by the Canadian Government, included in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The Grand Trunk loan? No, that is not in at all. That $15,000,000 loan to the-Grand Trunk is in the books of the Government without having any interest added to it from the time it was first lent. It stands there simply as a liability, and the arbitrators will have to take it into consideration as a liability against the company when they are valuing the road.
Do I understand the minister to say that he had a more recent statement than this contained in the blue-book?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: No. I said I was just reading off the statement I gave to-day.
Is that being presented today. for the first time?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: This statement is of December 31, 1918, and I asked for a statement of all the liabilities right u|p to date, and the amount is only a little more than the amount shown in this statement.
About how much difference is there?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: About $2,000,000 or
That is up to date?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes.

(position. The figures were compiled by the deputy minister and his staff. I asked the deputy minister to bring the statement right up to date the other day. But there is very little difference in the figures.
The most recent statement was the one you read to-day?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes.
What was the total of the statement the minister read this afternoon?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
It was $205,190,017.52.
To that had to be added $60,833,332.51 of guaranteed stock, making a total of $266,023,750.03. All the details were put on Hansard.
That statement only relates to the parent company?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: And its subsidiary companies, but did not include the Grand Trunk Pacific.

There are two items on page 40 I should like explained., the item of $806,600 common stock of the International Bridge Company held by the public, and $808,900 of common stock of the Central Vermont Railway held by the public.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: That is common stock held by the public. It was not included in my statement, because it is not a liability.
Are those two items included in the $180,000,000 that will be arbitrated on?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: No.
I cannot quite understand what will become of this stock. It must be an asset.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: We have not guaranteed it- It is held by the public and is not included in the stock that will be submitted to arbitration.
This stock must be held by part of the Grand Trunk system.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: It is outstanding over and above our own stock. We are only purchasing the stock of the original parent company. If there is any stock of the two companies mentioned held by the public, it will continue to be held by the public. The public own a certain amount of common stock in a number of different companies.
In addition to the $15,000,000 advanced to the Grand Trunk-page 39- are there any amounts due by the Grand Trunk Pacific which will also be included in the arbitration?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
No. The Grand Trunk Pacific is a subsidiary company and, of course, its assets and liabilities will all be taken into consideration by the arbitrators, but the only liabilities the Grand Trunk Pacific has are those towards the Government and the Grand Trunk. vestigate why the Drayton-Acworth report showed the Grand Trunk to have received $3,413,699.20 more than my statement showed they had received. My statement showed the amount to be $15,142,633.13. speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Iif the hon. member will read further he will see that the total liabilities of the Grand Trunk Pacific amount to $216,253,111. This will all be arbitrated in connection with the Grand Trunk system. There is considerable money already advanced by the Government, and it will be taken into consideration in the arbitration.

speechtext: It is really a mortgage, In valuing the road the arbitrators will naturally take into account all the liabilities, no matter to whom they are due, and we are entitled to place that as a liability against the Grand Trunk Railway Company.

speechtext: Yes.
What is the total amount of the indebtedness of the Grand Trunk Pacific to the Dominion Government?

Hence we are in the same 'position as if we were paying the $216,000,000, with this difference: That we do not have to borrow the money, but in so far as our liabilities, in so far as the credit of the country, and in so far as the putting up of the guarantee is concerned, we are bound to the extent of the sum mentioned. speechtext:
I am not arguing in favour
of Mr. Smith's report. I was proceeding to argue that the Government of the day that made the bargain with the British shareholders who own the Grand Trunk railway, protected the rights of the people of Canada by tying the Grand Trunk up tight, and to-day we are not here looking after the interests of the British shareholders who made a bargain with the Government, we are here looking after the interests of the people of Canada. It might be wise for the Government to look after the interest of the taxpayers of Canada and allow Sir Alfred Smithers and his Board of Directors to look after the interests of the British or Dutch or German shareholders or whoever may own shares of the Grand

Trunk Railway Company. That is their business. They made a bargain with this country in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific, and they gave certain guarantees. My judgment is that they should live up to those guarantees, and if they cannot live up to them, then let us do the same as any business ' man would do. Men come out to this country from Great Britain or Germany or Holland, and look for an investment. One man puts his money into railways; another man puts his money into real estate; another man puts his money into manufacturing. Is the Government going to step in and release from his obligations every man who makes a bad bargain? If the Government is going to take care of the man who puts his money into railways, it is just as much bound to protect the man who puts his money into real estate, or mines, or manufacturing, if he makes a bad bargain.
I want to come back again to the subsidiary companies that are not at all in Canada, that are in the United States where there is a large mileage of the Grand Trunk railway. Some of them go down through Vermont and part of New Hampshire; some run through Maine; some go into Michigan, and some into Illinois and Indiana. In this blue-book containing memoranda respecting the Grand Trunk Railway Company acquisition, there is at pages 54 and 55, a statement of the deficits on these roads in 1917. In 1917, the Central Vermont railway showed a deficit of $154,729; the Atlantic and St. Lawrence railway showed a deficit of $1,272,496; and the western subsidiary companies-that is, the Detroit, Grand Haven and Milwaukee, the Grand Trunk and Western, the Toledo, Saginaw and Muskegon-showed a deficit of $1,302,154. Adding these together, you get a total deficit of $2,729,379 on the subsidiary companies which the Government proposes to turn over to the people of Canada-subsidiary companies that are operating outside of this Dominion, that are operating in the United States. What does that total deficit of $2,729,379 represent? We are inviting the people of Canada to-day to subscribe to a Victory Loan at five and-a-half per cent, and if we capitalize the deficits on these roads in 1917, we find that we are inviting the people of Canada to subscribe for $49,625,072. That is the amount of money that represents the deficits which this Government is proposing to turn over to the people of Canada in the subsidiary companies of the Grand Trunk railway as of the year 1917. I submit to my hon. friends in all seriousness: Would

it not Be well to pay a little attention to the taxpayers of Canada? It has been quite apparent this afternoon that even the members of the Government, including the Minister of Railways and the President of the Council who have had this matter before them and have been looking into it for more than a year, are not quite clear on the whole situation. Would it not be well to say to Sir Alfred Smithers: In view of conditions throughout this country and the echoes coming in from the different provinces, we do not feel justified in going on with this bargain; we do not believe that the taxpayers of the Dominion are prepared to shoulder this burden, and you had better live up to your contract made with the previous Government. If they cannot live up to that contract, let them go into liquidation if necessary. It would not be the first time that railways have gone into liquidation on this continent; receiverships are not new in railway experience.
I have a statement here shoeing that in, 1910 thirty-nine railways in the United States went into the hands of a receiver, in 1913 forty-nine, and in 1915, eighty-five railways with a .mileage of 23,834. Will any one tell me that the United States suffered because of these railways going into the hands of a receiver? They were able to weed these roads out, and that is the only correct basis of dealing with this Grand Trunk muddle. It is a muddle and the deeper we go into it the more muddled it seems. I appeal to my friends opposite to take a little more interest in the taxpayers of Canada and a little less interest in the shareholders overseas, because their directors will take care of their interests.
