If the Grand Trunk Company were to be liquidated this debt would be preferred as against the four per cent guaranteed stock of the company.
If the assets of the company should not be sufficient to pay all the debts, the debt of Canada should be paid in preference to the four per cent guaranteed stock amounting to $60,000,000. Is it not a great advantage for the country to have a preference for the payment of its debt against the Grand Trunk over the $60,000,000 of guaranteed stock? We are simply inverting the position, as a result of which this $60,000,000 of guaranteed stock will have a prefer-

The motion of the hon. member (Mr. Denis) deals with what I regard as the gravest objection to this measure if we follow it out in detail. Every argument that can be advanced about the arbitration on the value of the preference and common stocks, can be applied with equal or greater force in the case of the guaranteed stock. There is danger in respect to this arbitration on $180,000,000 of preference stock and common stock. There is so much danger in it that it has alarmed some hon. gentlemen opposite. The hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) confessed the other day that he was very

much disturbed over the matter, but he informed us that after having talked with some person-he said that he would not betray secrets by naming him, but somebody-in very close relation to the Government- he was in a position to say that we would have an opportunity of scanning the details of this matter at a later stage of the discussion; in other words, that we were to have the agreement submitted to this House. My hon. friend was lured into a support of the measure by an assurance of that kind. He knows now that that assurance, if it was intended to be an assurance, was entirely unwarranted, because we have received the statement to-night that this agreement will not be submitted to the House, and that my hon. friend is not going to have an opportunity of scanning the terms to which he attached such great importance.
It is an alarming thing, especially in the light of some other arbitrations, to think that $180,000,000 of this stock, of various kinds, of the Grand Trunk is to be submitted to the uncertainties of arbitration. The danger is the uncertainty. But when you come to the guaranteed stock there is no uncertainty; the danger is the absolute certainty that the Dominion of Canada is going to be made to pay up to at least $30,000,000 more than the fair value of the stock. There is no room for any question about that. I submit it to any business man in this House. Here is a stock called the guaranteed stock-not guaranteed by any government; it is merely a phrase used by the Grand Trunk, the stock is guaranteed by the Grand Trunk. The ordinary market value of that stock was 40 to 50 a short time ago. A few days ago I gave quotations showing that it had advanced to 48. We are going to give that stock a four per cent guarantee of the Government of Canada. This agreement is going to make the Government of Canada pay forever four per cent on that stock, unless they care to redeem it by paying the capital amount thirty years hence. A stock which was 45 or 48 a month ago is going to be made by this Act of Parliament worth 90. There is no escape from that. A four per cent guarantee by the Government of Canada is worth in ordinary times par and more than par, but these are not ordinary times; money is high. I am taking it at an ordinary figure. When this transaction is consummated, and when this stock is no longer the guaranteed stock of the Grand Trunk but the guaranteed stock of the Government of Canada, it is going to be worth 85 or 90, and the difference be-

tween its fair value a month ago and the value which is to be given) to it by what we are doing will be nearly $30,000,000 of the money of the people of Canada. There is no hon. gentleman sitting there who, if he were dealing with a personal transaction, would not say that it was a monstrous thing.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend has conjured up a bugaboo in connection with this transaction iand has sought to convey the impression that this means a serious loss to the people of Canada. One has only to look at the transaction to see how incorrect my hon. friend's view is. The question of how the value of these stocks should be distributed between the different classes of stockholders is of no importance to the people of Canada. It makes no difference whatever in so far as the people are concerned whether the whole of the compensation goes to the holders of the guaranteed stock or is distributed among the guaranteed, preference and common stock holders. The only question in which we are concerned is the total amount that should be paid. That is the one thing that concerns the people of Canada. My hon. friend knows that if we made a cash offer to-day of $2,500,000 annually, and it is on record by the statement of Mr. Smithers and the Grand Trunk themselves, every dollar of it would go to pay the dividend on this guaranteed stock. If we were to offer $2,500,000 as an immediate cash offer, which we have offered, every dollar would go to the guaranteed stock because this guaranteed stock takes priority over all the preference and common stocks both in the matter of dividends and in the distribution of assets if the company were liquidated.
The Grand Trunk, referring to the Government's offer of $2,500,000 for the first three years, put the situation in this way: that this offer would mean the payment in full of the guaranteed stock immediately. In other words, if the Grand Trunk accepted the cash offer of $2,500,000 as the minimum offer for the first three years, it would do exactly what we are now doing: it would pay interest at four per cent on the total amount of this guaranteed stock, and it would place this stock in exactly the same position as it will be placed by reason of the guarantee. The whole question is this: is this stock worth the $2,500,000 annually in interest and is it worth possibly something more? The Government believes it is worth that and that we are safe in assuming the guarantee of this interest. We offered cash;
the Grand Trunk refused the cash. We not only offered this amount of cash, but we offered more. We offered, after the end of three years, $3,000,009 for four years; we offered $3,600,000 after that in perpetuity. The Grand Trunk refused that. They said it was confiscation if any one of these terms were imposed upon them. What we have done, so far as regards the minimum cash payment which we offered of $2,500,000, which would have paid four per cent on this stock,-we have guaranteed that. It does not add one dollar to the obligations which this country will have to pay because it will go towards the payment of the interest on this stock. Let me put it this way: if we arbitrated the guaranteed as well as the other stocks and if the award for this guaranteed stock, preference stock, and common stock, was $2,500,000 per annum, then it would all have to go, as the Grand Trunk President himself states, to this guaranteed stock-all that guaranteed stock would be in exactly the same position as it is to-day. I am quite aware, as everybody knows, that the effect of the Government's guarantee has been to appreciate to some extent that stock; but it does not add anything to the obligations which the people of Canada will be called upon to pay. We submit these facts to the consideration of the House and we maintain that the agreement is perfectly fair. One other consideration and I am through: anybody would know that stock under such conditions would appreciate to some extent on the market. It has a chance for appreciation just as the stock appreciated when the agreement with reference to the Grand Trunk Pacific went into effect. As a matter of expediency, we would have preferred to arbitrate the whole thing. But we could not get an agreement for arbitration on a satisfactory basis, unless we agreed to provide lor the guaranteed stock in this way. We believed the stocks were worth this amount and that this amount should be applicable to the guaranteed stock. That 9 p.m. is where the law would make it applicable in any case, and we consented that it should be so applicable.
Let me say in conclusion, that the Government has taken the position, and I submit it is a fair position, that the Grand Trunk railway, which has lines of feeders throughout Ontario and Quebec, should not pass into the harms of the Canadian Pacific Company.	.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes, we have taken the position that the Grand Trunk railway should not pass into the hands of other railway interests which would be adverse io those of the people of Canada. Separation of the Grand Trunk Pacific and the National Transcontinental from the Grand Trunk would not only be a colossal blunder, it would be a national crime, because you would impose upon the Government of Canada the obligation of maintaining a railway which, separated from its feeders, could not be made a financial success. No wonder Mr. Beatty said they did not wish to assume the Grand Trunk if they had to take it with the obligations of the Grand Trunk Pacific and he added that they did not want the Grand Trunk Pacific because it paralleled their line. I say it would be nothing short of a national crime to take away from the Grand 'Trunk Pacific and the National Transcontinental the only system of railways which can possibly make them a success. I care not what the motives may be that inspire my hon. friends opposite, in the course they are pursuing but if it were successfull, then it would make government operation of railways in Canada a colossal failure and would enable private interests from one end of this country to the other to say that public ownership could never be made a success in Canada. I care not what the motives of my hon. friends may be in opposing this legislation; their course would not only render public ownership a lamentable failure but would involve this country in the loss of millions of dollars in operating great stretches of railway without the feeders necessary to their success.
What further? If this railway passed out of our hands and into the hands of the other great railway controlling the situation in Ontario and Quebec, you would find in these two provinces a reproduction of the conditions which the people of Manitoba and Western Canada faced more than twenty years ago. My hon. friends know that the situation in Western Canada, when that country was held in the grip of a railway monopoly, was such that it almost produced an incipient rebellion. Are we to sit quietly here and see a railway monopoly established throughout Ontario and Quebec and see the people of these provinces forced into the position in which Manitoba found herself some years ago? The Government is fighting the battle for the people of Canada to give them a fair chance for honest competition in railway management and honest competition in railway accommodation. My 
hon. friends know that the men who are interested in defeating this legislation are only too happy to see it defeated whether the means employed be dilatory means, the postponement of consideration, or by actual opposition to the Bill. I do not wish to question the right of a man who is honestly opposed to public ownership under all considerations to oppose this Bill, blit if he is not honestly opposed to public ownership under every possible condition the present agreement is one that should be supported by him as well as by the people of Canada as a whole. *

Once more, Mr. Chairman, for the twentieth time in this debate, the President of the Privy Council, absolutely unable to meet the point at issue, draws a red herring across the trail in order that he may divert attention from the real question which is involved.
Oh, oh.

We are discussing the motion made 'by an hon. member in the form of an amendment. That motion does not discuss the question nor the principle of public ownership. We have had that discussed again and again; but whenever we bring up any matter bearing directly on one part of this transaction, and especially if it is a weak and defenceless portion, the hon. gentleman rushes in with an impassioned declaration in favour of public ownership. The hon. gentleman talks a good deal about motives; there is good ground for suspicion of motives in this matter when the hon, gentleman pursues a course so utterly lost to all reason and logic. Again the hon. gentleman brings in the bugaboo of the Canadian Pacific. The amendment has nothing to do with the Canadian Pacific. Why does the hon. gentleman again draw in that bugaboo? I repeat what I said the other night, and the hon. gentleman knows it is true-the Canadian Pacific cannot get this property unless it comes to the Parliament of Canada and obtains the necessary authority. The hon. gentleman knows that and yet, again and again, he drags in this bugaboo of the Canadian Pacific, hoping that the public would not understand this camouflage of the whole miserable transaction.
Mr. ROWELL; Will the hon. gentleman permit me. to ask him one question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If the Canadian Pacific Railway Company came to this Parliament

for legislation of that kind, would the hon. gentleman approve it?

There is another sample of my hon. friend's logic. It will he time enough when the Canadian Pacific comes here to consider that.
Some hon. MEMBEES: Oh, oh.
Would the hon. gentleman himself approve of it?
No, I would not. I would not he a member of a government which would put in the hands of one railway company corporation, a monopoly of the transportation of the country.

If that be true, then what becomes of the great principle of public ownership which my hon. friend champions? If the principle of public ownership .is as great and as holy as he represents it ,to be, why does he draw the line and say: ''We will grab the Grand Trunk, but we won't take the Canadian Pacific"? When the hon. gentleman says that he would not. take the Canadian Pacific he is abandoning his whole argument in respect to public ownership.
Pardon me; my hon. friend has certainly misunderstood me. I said that I would not approve of the Canadian Pacific taking the Grand Trunk. That was the question, and that is what I said.

It will be time enough to deal with that question, I repeat, when it comes up; it is not here now.
Some hon. MEMBEES: Oh, oh.

What hon. gentleman who says "Oh" would undertake to determine what he is going to do in a session of the Parliament of Canada which is yet to be held? I have an open mind on every question that comes before Parliament. I am not going to commit myself on any question which is for the next Parliament; I will see the measure when it comes and deal with it on its merits.
Again and again the President of the Council has dragged the Canadian Pacific railway into the discussion. He has done it so often and so clearly without warrant that there is a well-grounded suspicion that he cannot maintain his position in respect to this matter; that he cannot defend this bargain on its merits. The other ruight I was trying to find out where the urgency came in, and I asked the President of the Council to bring down any correspondence which showed that the Grand Trunk Eail-way Company were seeking to get rid of
their road. But there has not been a line to show anything of the sort; the urgency, as I pointed out, is entirely on the part of the Government who are trying to grab the Grand Trunk. When the hon. gentleman was asked for an explanation of the alleged urgency, what did he say? "Oh," he said, "iif we do not do this thing now, public opinion will be organized against it." I wonder whether the hon. gentleman realized the force of the admission that he then made. If we do not put this Bill through now, the people of Canada will have time to understand it, and if they understand it he is afraid that they will not approve of it. What was my honourable friend's argument in reply to that suggestion? He made an observation just as he was moving that the committee rise; I had no opportunity of noting it at the moment. Answering the argument-a reasonable argument, I think -that I advanced, he intimated that he was not afraid of legitimate public opinion. He said:
My hon. friend knows the influence of corporations in the past in carrying on organized propaganda, apposing or supporting legislation. Members of this House and the people of the country know what has happened in that regard in past years.
The honourable gentleman has no right to talk in terms of mystery. What does he mean by that statement? He is not afraid of public opinion, but he is afraid of some corporation. He is afraid of some corrupt influence being exerted-upon whom? Upon the men who sit around him? Who are the men who are going to be bribed and corrupted by the Canadian Pacific Eailway Company if this proposal does not go through at this time? I ask my honourable friend to give an explanation of that mysterious statement. He is not afraid of public opinion, but he is afraid of some corporation, and the corporation which he has spoken of again and again is the Canadian Pacific Eailway Company. What does he mean when he .suggests that that great Company is going to bribe Ihe members of this Parliament or the people of this country? There is no explanation of it at all; the honourable member owes an immediate explanation to the country. He has placed^ on record his belief that if this transaction does not go through now, public opinion will be aroused in this country against it. Am I not stating the case exactly? Is that not what he said? Then when we asked: why should not public opinion be organized against it? he says: I am not afraid of legitimate public opinion,

but I am afraid of the corrupting influence of the corporation. I think that he owes it to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to withdraw that remark, for it can have but one meaning-that the Canadian Pacic Railway Company will bribe members of this Parliament to defeat this Bill.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not know whether my honourable friend was in the House at the time, but the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) raised that question this afternoon and I gave my answer then; it is on record. My hon. friend's remarks are not justified by anything I said.

I regret that I was not present, but I think that all I have said to-day is fair and reasonable; it, too, will stand on Hansard.	'
Now, we come back to the real question, the question of the amendment before the committee. The hon. gentleman talks a great deal about the distribution of moneys in this transaction. We are not concerned about the distribution of moneys. This transaction is not a bulk transaction. For the purpose of our present discussion; for the purpose of considering the motion of my hon. friend, we do not need to go back into the correspondence; all the facts are before us in this Bill.
Several classes of stocks are to be acquired, and it is proposed that certain classes of these stocks shall be acquired by arbitration. We must deal with these latter classes on their merits; they form one section of the financial transaction. We are to have them dealt with by arbitration There is risk in it and danger in it, but at all events we understand how it is to be done.
Now, we come to another class of stocks, and let us not mix it up with the others; there is no question of distribution about it. The other class of stock is the four per cent guaranteed stock, so-called, of the Grand Trunk Railway Company; and we are going to make that a guaranteed stock of the Government of Canada. I am obliged to repeat myself on that point. That slock was worth on the market something under 50-48J was the quotation 1 read from a London paper. We are going to give that stock, by this proposal, a value of 85 or 90; and that stock is being traded in the London market to-day at huge profits to every one who touches it. You must look at this transaction separate and apart from all the others; you must not mix it up with the Canadian Pacific or with the other stocks or with any other
[Mr. Fielding. 1
thing. Here is a simple, straight transaction: you are going to take $61,000,000 of stock which a few days ago was worth only from 45 to 43-something under |60-and you are going to give that stock a value ol nearly 100-certainly 00-and the difference, representing about $30,000,000, is to go into the hands of speculators in London. There is no excuse for it; there is no defence for it; the public will not be misled by the dragging in of other questions. Who, looking at this proposal as a business man would, purely on its merits, would not say that it is utterly unsound and should not be carried out?

It was most unfortunate that the President of the Council .'(Mr. Rowell) should have lost his temper, because we were getting along very nicely and making some progress. More information was being given us by the Minister of Railways than by the President of the Council. I say this for the President of the Council: He has proved himself an exceptionally good lawyer. It is puzzling to us to know just whose brief he is holding. Is he holding a brief now for the Minister of the. Interior? Is he holding a brief for the Minister of Railways? Is he holding a brief for the Canadian Northern Railway? Or is he holding a brief for himself? He has shown in every way a degree of legal tact which is familiar to all students of law. Law students are generally told that if they see that they are getting the worst of a case their best course of procedure is to make a straw man, hammer at it, get vicious, hammer at it some more and frighten the other fellow. The President of the Council employed these tactics to-night very well. He built up a straw man that nobody was thinking of or speaking of-the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. Then, after hammering the Canadian Pacific for all he was "worth, he started to build up a second straw man -the motives actuating the Opposition in seeking information. Now, had he been interested just at the time the Minister of Railways was speaking he would have observed that the Minister of Railways gave a statement here to-day which was given for the first time. After persistent questioning upon a subject of paramount interest to the people of Canada, we succeeded in getting a revised edition of a statement which had previously been submitted.
I think I voice the sentiments of the whole Opposition when I say that in spite of all the lecturing of the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell), the Opposition is going to

continue to do its duty; it is going to stand by the people and for the people, and it is going to find out for the people just what they are being asked to sanction. If it takes another week to do that, and if the Government do not want to be frank and to come out with the whole statement, then we shall keep at the matter until we get the whole statement out, so that the people of this country who are going to be committed to an expenditure exceeding $500,000,000 will know what they are committed to. The President of the Council could have told us all that he had to tell us in a quiet manner; it was not necessary at all in telling us to get as mad as creatures that I dare not speak of in this House, but he tore up and tore down and he hammered, and one would wonder if he were really angry at certain results that were coming in to-day, or if he were disturbed by the statement made by the Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) that we were going to buy hotels by this agreement. Perhaps he had been seized of the possibility of the Government's taking over the Chateau Laurier, and it may be bothering him whether he will have to continue giving the right to hotels in certain quarters to sell liquor under a license, or, perhaps, to sell it without a license, or how long the Government may have to refrain from bringing down threatened prohibition legislation. I cannot work into the minister's mind, and I cannot for the life of me say what made him so mad to-night. It may be that the President of the Council, from moralist to preacher, from preacher to dictator, from dictator to democrat and from democrat to autocrat, has gone on and assumed a new phase, and I really believe that it may be summed up in this. The President of the Council has become an actor. Any man who can, on a question respecting the uplift of the whole of us, respecting the use of tobacco, for instance, get just as angry in this House as man ever could get, and work himself up into the state into which he worked himself to-night, must be an actor, or I do not know what an actor is. But with all that, it seems to me-and I hold no brief for any of my friends seated beside me-that the statement made by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) was very fair; it was simply seeking for information that could easily be given with a "yes" or "no," or with a few figures. It was not necessary at all to get angry about the matter. It is a mistake on the part of the Government to think that they are going to prevent us from getting a bold,
broad, statement of what this country is going to be committed to, by reading us curtain lectures. Words were uttered by a man whom I hold in very high esteem in this country, and perhaps with your permission, Sir, I may repeat them:
In the meantime while the Government is through the instrumentality of the public credit and otherwise, using every endeavour to alleviate conditions which have inevitably arisen out of the war and overcome the effects of the sudden cessation of the activities which it created it is the clear duty of all citizens to earnestly co-operate with the Government and with one another to the end that with the exercise of patience, goodwill, and high patriotic spirit we may tide over successfully, this most trying and critical period in the national life of the Dominion.
The gentleman. (Sir Thomas White) who uttered these words occupied the position of Minister of Finance, and he used them as part of his Budget speech in June last, in this very House. I ask hon. gentlemen now who have some thought and concern for the rights of the people of this country, who did not, a few months ago, when the leader of the Opposition moved his amendment, vote away the last vestige of the rights of the people, to consider well those words uttered by the ex-Minister of Finance, and to give approval to the amendment now moved by the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Denis). What does this amendment mean? It means simply to throw the whole thing before the arbitrators and to let them place a value upon it. We have been told time and again that we must pay this 4 per cent on the guaranteed stock and that we must pay the 4 per cent on the debenture stock, but that the rest will all be arbitrated. The hon. member for Joliette places a fair proposal before the House. I ask the House to adopt it because then, at least, the country will know what is the proposition before it, and the country is certainly not aware of the liabilities that are being assumed today.

The amendment moved
by the hon. member (Mr. Denis) is in exact accord with the recommendation of the Drayton-Acworth report which has been cited here as the authority of the Government for going on with this legislation. The President of the Council made no reply whatever to the amendment. I should like to ask the Government what was the cause of their receding from the original suggestion of the Drayton-Acworth report? That should be made plain to the country. The President of the Council said that they suggested arbitration. Person-

ally I think the suggestion in the Drayton-Acworth report was a very generous one, perhaps too generous. Until we know the value of the assets of this undertaking we are rather reckless in making any offer of an annuity to the shareholders of that company, but since it was made, and the Drayton-Acworth report was cited as an authority for making that proposal, why did the Government depart from that report in this matter? The President of the Council wished to impute motives to the Opposition, to try to imply that the Opposition were opposing this for motives that were not, perhaps, honourable. Instead of that it looks very much to me as if there were a nigger on the fence in this proposition. There is absolutely no reason why this $60,000,000 worth of stock should be set aside until we have valued the assets of the Grand Trunk undertaking, and until the arbitrators make a valuation. Why is this stock set aside? The Government tell us that the Grand Trunk would not agree on any other terms. The Grand Trunk Railway Company have never admitted their liabilities to the Government on account of the Grand Trunk Pacific guarantee.
They did not want to accept this $3,600,000 until that matter was straightened out. The Government made a counter-proposal to submit the whole thing to arbitration, and it is just possible that if it were submitted to arbitration, instead of $2,500,000, $3,000,000 or $3,600,000 there would have been nothing to pay on account of this stock purchase. I cannot understand why the Government and honourable gentlemen opposite are so anxious to spend $60,000,000 at this time when there is absolutely no ground for the transaction and when they have absolutely no authority for it. The Government tell us that the Grand Trunk people owe us $97,000,000 and .also have owed us $15,000,000 for 50 years, and in the face of that they say: Before we undertake to collect our debts from the Grand Trunk, before we undertake to look after the interest of the people of Canada, we will guarantee the interest of the Grand Trunk stock to the amount of $60,000,000. In other words, their means of collecting the bill is first to give the Grand Trunk more money. There is absolutely no sound business in that and absolutely no reason for it, and I am satisfied that it will not stand the light of day in the country. I therefore shall vote for the amendment.
Amendment, Mr Denis, negatived; yeas 25, nays, 49.

Mr. -I. D. REID:	You are not.

When you jcome into

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I have already explained it. The Grand Trunk Pacific Branch Lines Company spent $29,186,593 on road and equipment. They issued bonds to the extent of $16,786,440 that were guaranteed by the local governments. Other amounts have been expended on that construction for which bonds have not been issued. They simply carried the amounts as a liability instead of issuing bonds. It is a liability against the Branch Lines Company, which is a. subsidiary of the Grand Trunk Pacific.
Does the minister say that these branch lines will not be taken over?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes.
You assume the liability?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes, of course.
Then, am I to add that to the $501,000,000 and the $26,000,000 to arrive at the total liabilities?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member can add anything he likes, but it will be like adding broomsticks and oranges. They are in different classes altogether. I do not know whether another statement to the same effect will be of any assistance to the hon. gentleman or not. This is the Grand Trunk Pacific Branch Lines Company. It is a child of the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk Pacific is the child of hon. gentlemen opposite, and those hon. gentlemen may get considerable satisfaction now by deriding the child of their child. I do not know that the Grand Trunk Pacific Branch Lines Company is something that we should avoid simply because that company has liabilities. Every com' pany in the world that does any business has liabilities.
Have they not assets?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, of course. The
assets are set out on the other side of the ledger. A child can see them, and he who runs may read. What more explanation the wit of man can give -than is there I am at a loss to know. Every statement of every company is given in the same form. Yrou cannot add the liabilities of the Branch Lines Company, owned by the Grand Trunk Pacific, to the liabilities of the Grand Trunk Pacific,

owned by the Grand Trunk, and make all a part of the liabilities of the Grand Trunk. That is what my hon. friend would like to do, and I presume that in his mind it is all right. But in the mind of any one who wants to address this question honestly it is not all right. What we assume are the liabilities of the parent company that we take. When you have stated the full liabilities of the parent company you have stated the limit of our obligations, and so far as the direct obligation goes we are liable only for the debenture stock and guaranteed stock. Certainly these companies have liabilities, but they have assets against them.

The minister may take a certain degree of delight in entertaining himself and his friends behind him, hut I may tell him that to-day we got very much further than his statement. The question was put and answered in a way as to what the total liabilities of the undertaking amount to.	_

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Then, what more does the hon. gentleman want?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: They are not included because they should not be. That is the answer.

I find also in this government publication the following:
Southern New England Railway.
Under construction. Information at hand is very incomplete. In May, 1916, the Central Vermont Railway got authority to issue $30,000,000 of bonds, bearing guarantee of Grand Trunk Railway Company, but what portion, if any, of- this issue was made, it cannot he said.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Where is the hon. member reading from?
I am more generous than the hon. gentleman's friend to his right, and I will give him the page. It is 51.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: There is no information other than that which is contained in the report.

My hon. friend is coming to this Parliament on that kind of a statement when we are guaranteeing the bonds of a company in the United States to the extent of $30,000,000 and he does not know any more about it than that it was stated that some three years ago these bonds were guaranteed. His official report says that he does not know what amount has been sold. He does not know anything more about it than that they guaranteed $30,000,000 for a road in the United States, and he asks this House to pass this legislation. Some hon. members on the Government side have insisted that there must be some other motive behind the opposition to this measure than a desire to get this information for the Canadian people. It looks as if there was some other motive behind hon. gentlemen opposite than a desire to protect the people's interest.
The Minister of Railways made the statement to-night that we were going to take over the branch lines. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes.

What did the President of the Council mean by making the statement a short time before that we would only take over such branch lines as would be profitable to the Government?
Mr. J, D. REID:	I am sorry that the
President of the Council had to leave to take a train and that he is not here to answer for himself. I did not understand the President of the Council to make that statement, but I understood him to say that we would take over the branch lines which

the Grand Trunk owned, controlled or operated.

The President of the Council said that the taking over of the Grand Trunk and- Grand Trunk Pacific did not imply that we had to take over the branch lines. I recognized the argument of the Minister of the Interior about the parent company as being sound. Then I marvelled at the statement of the President of the Privy Council that we were only responsible for the branch lines that we took over and that the Government was not bound by this legislation or by any agreement to take over the subsidiary lines of the Grand Trunk or the Grand Trunk Pacific.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am glad the hon. gentleman realizes the soundness of my position on the main point. As to what the President of the Council may have said, while I was not here, it would be strictly correct. The Government in becoming the owners of the Grand Trunk do not assume any obligations except such as the contract calls for. The Grand Trunk would be under certain obligations and would be the owner of certain companies. If the Grand Trunk, for example, hold the stock of a company and it were found that the liabilities of that company were greater than its assets and it did not serve the public, say, in Canada, so as to make it our duty to run the company, we would not be compellable to run it, because no such obligation is embodied in our contract. There might be a branch line in the United States; if we found that its liabilities exceeded its assets we would be under no obligation whatever to take over the road or to have anything to do with it. The Grand Trunk Pacific branch lines are owned by the Grand Trunk Pacific Branch Lines Company. These are in Canada and they are valuable branch lines. They are lines running through the Canadian West where communities have been built up and necessarily these lines must be operated. There is no reason to doubt that these roads are well worth what is against them, and in taking over this stock there is not very much liability on our part. We assume everything when we take the stock of the parent company. When you state the obligations that we assume that is the end of it. I hope that is clear to my hon. friend.

It is perfectly clear to me, and I have no doubt that if I made the statement that the President of the Council had said the very reverse my hon. friend would have argued that the President of
the Council was right with the same ability that he has just displayed in arguing that if the President of the Council did make the statement he was perfectly right.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He is.
The Minister of the Interior will not say, as the President of the Council said this afternoon, that in taking over the parent company we are not taking over the subsidiary companies.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We take the right to take them all, but it does not entail the obligation to do so.
Then if we are taking the right to take them what is the statement of the present liabilities which we can tell the people, or which we can tell our own electors, we are assuming?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman were to tell his people that, would not his people say:	How are we liable unless we
assume the liability?-we have the right to do so but if it does not pay us to do so we will not do it. The people are not going to be seriously affected when they do know what we-guarantee here and they have a right to know what it is. We have told the hon. gentleman that over and over and over again.

But we have a different
statement to-night.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: You never got anything different. If the hon. gentleman will show me any two statements that will conflict I will be very glad to-

If the hon. gentleman
reads Hansard to-morrow he will see that the Minister of Railways brought down a brand new statement to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The statement may be new but the facts will be old.

There were certain brand new facts and I am sure the Minister of the Interior did not see them because the Minister of Railways told us that he got them direct from his deputy minister as being brand new and up to date.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If he got them there
they will he right.

They want to tell the
people of Canada that these are the facts; brand new facts, correct facts. Therefore I ask the Minister of Railways to say now, in view of the fact that there is a difference of opinion between the Minister of the Interior and the President of the Council what

the situation is. I would not say that the ministers would differ from each other when they were both here because they would get their statements to coincide very quickly. But whilst one was absent there was a direct difference of opinion, a direct difference of statement, putting a totally different aspect upon the liabilities that we are going to assume. Now I ask the Minister of Railways does that change the brand-new statement that he gave the House to-day?
Mr. J. D. REID; No, it does not.

Before this clause, which I regard as the fundamental clause of the Bill, is adopted I wish to say a few words in the performance of my duty to my constituents. Speaking upon the Bill a few days ago I cited a resolution passed by the Board of Trade of St. John protesting against the acquisition of the Grand Trunk Railway under present conditions. We have been assured by hon. gentlemen opposite that we are opposing the passage of this Bill in defiance to public opinion. Well, public opinion-, as far as has been expressed in any quarter at all,.has been in opposition to the acquisition of the Grand Trunk unde^- present conditions. My hon. friend from Royal (Mr. H. H. McLean) who spoke forcibly on this question a few days ago, pointed out, as I did, the nature of the resolution which the Board of Trade at -St. John, N.B., had passed. That resolution is still in effect; it has not been rescinded. Late on Saturday I received from the secretary of the Board of Trade of Bathurst, in the county of Gloucester, a copy of -a resolution- which I deem it to he my duty to read in order that it may appear in Hansard. That resolution, which is signed by Mr. Joseph B. Storer, secretary of the Board, reads as follows:
Bathurst, N.B., October 24,1919. A special meeting of the Bathurst Board of Trade was held here last night when the following resolution was passed unanimously :
" Resolved that the Bathurst Board of Trade has heard with regret that the Federal Government has now under consideration a Bill for the purchase by the Dominion of the Grand Trunk Railway system. That the deficits of government railways last year amounted to over thirty-one million dollars. That the opinion of the Board is that so soon after the war the time is not opportune to add a very large sum to the national debt by the purchase of a railway system having Portland, Maine, as a port and thereby discriminating against Maritime Province ports. That the United States and Great Britain furnished positive proof that the government operation of railway systems entails greater 
expenditure than without. The Bathurst Board of Trade respectfully submits that the said Bill be deferred until the question is submitted to the people with the facts."
Mr. -Storer adds the following comments:
I	may- say that this was a very representative meeting of the business men of Bathurst, was attended by adherents of all political parties, and is considered to be representative of the opinion of a large majority of the people of the constituency of Gloucester.
This resolution, I may say, expresses the opinion not only of the people of Bathurst but also of the population of the northern part of the province of New Brunswick.
The House has already had an
II	p.m. expression from the people of
St. John and southern New Brunswick; and to-day there has been another expression of opinion from the constituency of Victoria and- Carleton, New Brunswick. I believe the resolution from the Bathurst Board of Trade to be a correct expression of the feelings of the business men of that town. They wish the Government to wait before passing this legislation, the present time, when the financial conditions* of the country, after the war, are almost in a dangerous state, to use the language of the ex-Minister of Finance, not being opportune. Therefore there should be a postponement of this legislation until the question has- been submitted to the people.
I't- has been claimed by hon. gentlemen opposite that the present railway situation is a result of the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific. May I toe permitted to remind those hon. gentlemen that when the Liberal party left office the Grand Trunk Pacific and National Transcontinental railways were in a perfectly healthy condition and would have played a successful part in the development of the country had it not been for their successors who, when they entered office, adopted a policy calculated to divert all possible traffic from those lines, and not only that -but placed every possible obstacle in the way of finishing their construction, and by degrading the Grand-Trunk Pacific made it fail in successful operation. What was planned was to bring to our Maritime Provinces' ports the whole of the trade of the Prairie Provinces, by giving that traffic a shorter haul than any other line could offer and at the least expense possible. That these plans were wise and sagacious is shown by the fact that notwithstanding the obstacles pla-ced in the way of the successful operation of the road, grain -was carried from Winnipeg to the Maritime Province ports for a rate

four cents a bushel lower than any other line was alble to carry that traffic. Had the policy introduced by Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his colleagues for the development and successful operation of that route been as vigorously pressed as it should have been the railway situation in the country would not be what it is to-day. In this connection, the Gutelius investigation and the Gutelius report-a mass of stupid contradictions which no Canadian engineer of any eminence would have signed-will be remembered. Mr. Gutelius contradicted himself the following year when, in the enjoyment of his "mess of po'ttage," he asked with respedt to the Intercolonial railway from Moncton to Halifax and Sydney, for an appropriation of millions in order to take care of the traffic which existed between those points, and so as to make it possible to emjploy much larger trains for the hauling of that traffic: This is the reply I make when I hear it stated by hon. gentlemen opposite that the present railway situation is due to the maladministration of the Laurier Government. The Borden Government not only did all they could to delay the proper construction and operation of the Transcontinental from Winnipeg to Quebec and the Maritime Provinces, but did all in their power to divert traffic from Cochrane to Toronto. The Liberal party of that time had passed a resolution in favour of granting the British preference to imports passing through Maritime Province ports-, and that resolution was to be effective as regards the terminus of the Grand Trunk Pacific.
The Grand Trunk Pacific project was completed three or four years ago; yet the Government has not put into effect the terms of that resolution. Will they do it now? The resolution expresses the fear that Canadian trade will go through a port in Maine instead of through iSt. John and Halifax. I trust that the Government will take into consideration public opinion as it is ex-pressed from day to day. Public opinion indicates clearly that the conditions generally are unfavourable to the carrying out of this proposal at this time. The fact that this railway goes to a port on the American coast is detrimental to the maritime ports of Canada. I trust, therefore, that this matter will at least be deferred until next session in order that the people may give it more consideration; and, if this Government does not do so, that this House and the Senate will see to it that public opinion is respected. I do not fear the influence of any corporation-I am expressing my
opinions as I have expressed them consistently during the last fifteen years in regard to this matter of railways. Moreover, I have placed before the Committee the opinion of the Board of Trade of the town of Bathurst, in Gloucester county-a board composed chiefly, I may say, of leading Conservatives of that town.

A question was raised by the member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) a short time ago which deserves, I think, more attention than the Minister of Railways gave it. I refer to the guarantee of $30,000,000 mentioned on page 51 of the blue-book. I quote:
Besides the guarantees to the Grand Trunk
Pacific, the Grand Trunk railway have guaranteed the following.
A number of railways are mentioned, and we come down to the Southern New England railway:
Under construction. Information at hand is very incomplete. In May, 1916, the Central Vermont railway got authority to issue $30,000,000 of bonds, bearing guarantee of Grand Trunk Railway Company, but what portion, If any, of this issue was made, it cannot he said.
That is an extraordinary statement to make an connection with a business venture of this kind-ihat three and a half years ago the Central Vermont was authorized by the Grand Trunk Railway Company to issue bonds to the extent of $30,000,000 and to sell them to the public, and that at this day the Government is not able to ascertain whether those bonds were all issued or not or how many were issued. There must be something wrong with This statement. We know that whatever the number of bonds issued to the public, the Grand Trunk Railway system is bound to meet that obligation. I would like the minister to explain this paragraph; to tell us how many of these bonds were issued and why the Government is not able to tell whether the whole amount was issued or not.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman will look at page 35 of the blue-book he will ascertain just the relationship between the Central Vermont and the Grand Trunk. The statement says:
Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada controls Central Vermont Railway Company by majority stock ownership (72%). This com- ' pany owns 246.3 miles in U.S.A.
From the statement on page 51 it would appear that the Central Vermont received authority for an issue of $30,000,000 of bonds. It is only proper that information



as to whatever indirect liability there may be on that account upon the Grand Trunk be made known as dearly as possible. That information will he secured for the hon. gentleman. But if, say, half of those bonds were issued, the proceeds would be in the Central Vermont property in addition to the value of that property. If nothing at all was issued there would be no addition; if the whole thing was issued there would be that much addition. It cannot he said that it means just that much less value in the Grand Trunk. Presumably it means nothing less or nothing more, because the proceeds of whatever was issued would he there in the road, which is owned to the extent of seventy-two per cent by the Grand Trunk Eailway Company.

Everything depends on what the railway to he built with the proceeds of this issue is worth. If it is not worth the amount of the bonds, then the Grand Trunk would have to implement that liability. But we ought to know what the liability of the Grand Trunk in this respect is. The minister has not told us why it is difficult to get that information.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: There is no difficulty at ail.

Why is it not a matter of record?
Mr. J. I). EEID: We have given all the records that we have in the department. This statement was made from the official records in the department; if there is any further information that I can give I shall certainly get it. I shall take this matter up with the Grand Trunk officials in the morning and probably by to-morrow give the hon. gentleman in detail the information that he asks for. There is no desire at all to withhold it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Is the information not already of record in the statement that has been put on Hansard? The obligations in respect of the guarantees of the Grand Trunk Eailway system are all stated, and included in it is the Central Vermont railway. The interest rate is given as four per cent; outstanding bonds, $11,750,000; annual interest, $470,000. The par value of the stock owned by the company is given next. From that statement it appears that' the hon. gentleman's question is fully answered. The outstanding obligation in respect of which there is a Grand Trunk guarantee is, therefore, $11,750,000.
I understand that to be in addition to the $30,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No this is given as obligations in respect of guarantees of controlled or subsidiary companies. This *would be the total obligation in respect of which there is guarantee.
Then why is it stated in the blue book that it is impossible to obtain the information?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That statement was prepared earlier; the one that was put on record to-day is a more recent one.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: At the top of page 51 the hon. member will see the words "guarantees as at December 31st, 1917." That was almost two years ago; this other statement is up to date. '

The statement means a little more than the Minister of the Interior has indicated. I think it is a full confirmation of the view we have taken on this side of the House that this transaction of enormous magnitude, of most complicated character, affecting the accounts of many companies, is being thrust upon the House with absolutely inadequate information. In newspaperdom they have a fashion of giving prominence to a thing by setting it up, as they say, "in a box," where you can see it separate and apart from everything else.
I think the point to which the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) and the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. J. H. Sinclair) have been referring ought to be set up in Hansard "in a box". This is the statement which appears upon page 51 and upon which we have been voting. The minister, it is true, brought down something extra to-day, but in the meantime we have been voting on this blue-book, and on the faith of it some hon. gentlemen have been supporting this measure. On page 51, we find an official statement giving guarantees as of December 31, 1917, or nearly two years ago. That is, all the information which the [DOT]Government could bring down to us is two years old. We read:
Besides the guarantees to the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Grand Trunk Railway Company have guaranteed the following:
Then follow several railways. Then comes:
Southern New England railway. Under construction. Information at hand is very incomplete. In May, 1916, the Central Vermont railway got authority to issue $30,000,000 of bonds, hearing guarantee of Grand Trunk Railway Company, hut what portion, if any, of this issue was made, it cannot be said.
The Central Vermont is a subsidiary of the Grand Trunk. That statement should be set up "in a box"-a $30,000,000 transaction

concerning which the official information is simply that it is very incomplete. We cannot add anything.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: But it is added.

Does my hon. friend's statement which has been brought down today, but which has not been printed, refer to the Southern New England railway? I think what he read a moment ago referred to guarantees by the Grand Trunk of the Central Vermont.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, the Central Vermont.
But in this case the bonds would be issued by the Southern New England railway which would be a subsidiary of the Central Vermont, and the Central Vermont would be a subsidiary of the Grand Trunk.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Is it not the other way about? The bonds would not be issued by the Southern New England railway because the statement says that the Central Vermont railway got authority to issue these bonds, bearing guarantee of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. Then the statement following that shows the whole issue in respect of the Central Vermont railway, in respect of which there is a Grand Trunk guarantee. It is true the figures are not given here in respect of that one subsidiary line, but they are given in respect of the others. The information as of that date is pretty complete as regards the other roads. But all the information is not on page 51; the whole book is full of it, and in so far as it is incomplete in that one particular, it is made complete by this subsequent statement.
Is it the intention of the Government to have this new statement printed?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The statement is on
Hansard and, of course, it will be printed in Hansard to-morrow.

The whole business in connection with branch lines is very unsatisfactory. It appears that we are purchasing a very heavy liability in the United States, according to this blue-book. None of these railways is,, so far as we can learn, paying its way. If you look at page 27, you find the following:
United States affiliations-by book figures ol December 31, 1917, these roads show a deficit of $1,302,154. To this must be added deficit of Central Vermont of $154,729 not shown in Grand Trunk Railway Company's statement. This, however, does not show the deficit for the Atlantic and St. Lawrence which for 1917 was 90}
about $1,200,000. Thus making over $2,600,000 as the income cost to the Grand Trunk railway in 1917, for the American railways.
That is tc say, this group of railways, all in a foreign country, which railways we are going to place under our control and pay for, are losing money to the tune of $2,600,000 a year. That is what it looks like. That is public ownership with a vengeance. The people of Canada might be in favour of public ownership, but they are certainly not in favour of public ownership in a foreign country by which the taxpayers of this country have to pay $2,600,000 a year to keep those railways going.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member
knows, if he will consider a moment, that that is not the right way to state the matter at all. It is true that the Grand Trunk is in a foreign country. If the Grand Trunk were a system that were severable, it stands to reason that we would not be anxious to get the portion in a foreign country; we would be glad not to. But it is not severable; we cannot sever it and make it a system at all. Consequently, this has to be secured. While that might be the loss in respect of those American lines, that is made up again on the other side, and the whole is reflected in the final statement of the Grand Trunk Railway system, which final statement is really the matter in which the people of Canada and the members of this House are interested. That is the aggregate. In making up that aggregate, these deficits are taken into account and surpluses on other roads on the other side are taken into account, and the net result is there shown, so that it is wholly wrong to say that we are taking some sections there and that the people of Canada will be taxed in order to pay deficits upon them. The people of Canada get something against that, and one is set off against the other. The total shows a surplus, and it is the value of the stock on which the surplus arises that we are having arbitrated.

While I understand the difficulty of separating these roads, it seems that we are going to take over these roads in the United States for the benefit of Americans at a cost of upwards of $2,000,000 a year. That may be unavoidable, but it may be just as well to know that we are acting in that benevolent way and that that action is being taken by periple who formerly did not want to "have any truck or trade with the Yankees." It seems that we are very generous to pay $2,000,000 a year in ordei to give them cheap rates.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member has quite outdone his competitor from Guys-borough (Mr. Sinclair) in unfairness. There is nothing generous in this matter at all, nothing in the way of paying something for Americans; we are paying it wholly for ourselves. If this were not there, we would be paying just that much less; but this being there, there may be other roads here in respect of which we get a benefit for which we pay nothing as a consequence of this being there. I am not explaining this for the benefit of the hon. member for iShel-burne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) because his appreciation of anything of that sort is just as clear as inline, but why does he say that we are ashing the people of Canada to pay out between two and three million dollars in order that Americans may have railroad service? We are not doing anything of the sort nor anything that could with any approach to fairness be so *described.	(

I quite appreciate what the hon. member has said in regard to the difficulty of severing the undertaking, but there is no getting away from the fact that it is the people of Canada who are going to operate this road with a gain or a loss. It is debatable whether or not we are going to have a gain on the whole transaction, but it is the clearest thing in the world that there is a loss of over $2,000,000 on the American end of the Grand Trunk, and the people of Canada will have to pay that loss. There is no esoape from that.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
But does it not follow
that against that we get $2,000,000 for which we pay nothing at all?

Not from the United
States; we get it out of the ratepayers of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
But we get it instead
of the company, so that the thing is as broad as it is long.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
I suppose the Government
are taking over not only the trackage of the Grand Trunk system, but the engines and the cars, the equipment. Has the minister any data as to what proportion of .the engines, the motive power of the Grand Trunk, is owned by Blair & Co. and what proportion of the trucks are owned by the Columbia Trust Company?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I presume Blair &
Co., is a company associated with the Grand Trunk in equipment trusts. Is that the case? I have never heard the name before,
[Hr. Fielding.]
but I presume they issue equipment trusts, for that is the method by which the Grand Trunk, as any other company, owns its equipment subject to these equipment trusts, which are virtually mortgages against the equipment. I do not know just how much interest Blair & Co. have in the amount set out on page 39.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
I concluded that inasmuch
as the minister was taking over on behalf of the people of Canada a large railway as a going concern, well equipped with engines and freight and passenger cars, he would be able to tell the people of Canada what proportion of those engines was owned by Blair & Co. and what proportion of the trucks was owned by the Columbia Trust Company.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They own none of them.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Blair & Co. may hold the bonds against the equipment. Equipment trusts notes are shown on page 39, amounting to $6,092,999.91. The hon. member wants to know how much of those bonds are owned by Blair & Co, and how much by the Columbia Trust Company. That does not appear in this statement, but I have no doubt I can get it from the Grand Trunk people.

It is possible that these
two companies absolutely own part of the rolling stock?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They do not.

I am quite willing to take the minister's word, but when my hon. friend iMr. Robb asked him the question he did not know. It is a practice in the United States to lease engines, and we would like to know whether this rolling stock of the Grand Trunk is leased or purchased, what amount of rolling stock there is, and the liabilities against it. It is just possible that a large percentage of the rolling stock of the Grand Trunk is only leased. We should have all this information.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The company owns a large proportion of the equipment outright. It appears in the list of assets as Property invested in road and equipment, $434,990,999.37." The equipment is not shown separately, but I could get that information. The other amount representing equipment notes outstanding is for new equipment that has not been paid for, and against which there will be bonds. Some of these may be owned by Blair & Co. and some by the Columbia Trust Company. If the hon, gentleman will turn to page 38 he -will find

the amount invested in the road and equipment under the head of " Assets."
How can we tell how much was invested in equipment and how muon in the road?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I will get the hon. gentleman a statement in more detail.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: I think this is a matter of importance to the people of Canada The minister must have seen a great number of the engines on the Grand Trunk railway with a plate bolted on them labelled " Owned !by Blair & Co." It does not say "Bonded" or "Mortgaged," but "Owned by Blair & Co."

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: That is what they call equipment bonds.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: A number of the trucks also have a plate, " Owned by the Columbia Trust Company." Imagine the condition the Government would be in, if they took over the road and then Blair & Co. and the Columbia Trust Company said: "We own those trucks and we want them immediately," and then took possession of them. The minister should tell us under what conditions we are operating this equipment, and if it is leased, for how long?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Blair & Co. could not possibly take the engines in the way my hon. friend suggests. The engines are the property of the company and the bonds are simply a mortgage on the engines. They could never be taken so long as the interest and the agreed amount of principal is paid annually. The same applies to the Columbia Trust Company. Nearly all the railway companies, the Canadian Pacific, for instance, the Canadian Northern', and the Grand Trunk issue equipment bonds against their equipment at the time of purchase. You will see quoted on the market Canadian Pacific equipment bonds, Canadian Northern equipment bonds, etc. The cost of the equipment and the interest on it is a charge in connection with operation, and is not put in the list of liabilities against the road.

The clause we are discussing involves the taking over of the entire capital stock of the Grand Trunk with the exception of $12,500,000 of guaranteed stock. Have the Grand Trunk directors given the Government any assurance that the Grand Trunk has control of the entire capital stock of the company? I have frequently seen it stated in the newspapers that this stock is floating around in different countries, in Europe and elsewhere, and I have not heard the minister say anything on that question.
Have the directors of the Grand Trunk Company all the stock under their control in such a way that when the arbitration is completed they can turn it over to the Government, none of it being in the hands of private owners?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is, the stock we are arbitrating on?

I am referring to, all the stock. The guaranteed stock may be in the same position, but the common stock and the preference stock. That is the stock that is most likely to be scattered around. What will be the position if the directors of the Grand Trunk are not able to deliver the whole of that stock when the transaction is completed? Have they given an assurance to the Government that they will be able to deliver it?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have not heard of any assurance from the Grand Trunk that they have their hands on the stock and can at any fixed date deliver it. But a study of the Bill will disclose this situation: The Bill contemplates an agreement which must be ratified by the shareholders of the Grand Trunk; that is, by the holders of these very stocks in question.
A majority.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I should think that for a transaction of this kind it would require a two-thirds majority, but that is a question of law. Assume for the sake of argument that it is just a majority; it would mean that the company bound itself to deliver the stock. The Bill goes on to say that the agreement shall provide that any undelivered stock may be declared by the Governor in Council to be the property of the Government, and until it is delivered they have no rights at all. The rights of the company cease immediately on the declaration of the Governor in Council. We have jurisdiction to do that because it is a Canadian incorporated company, and in any event they accede to the exercise of that power. Consequently the country takes no chances in that regard at all. It may be some time before all the stock will have been searched out and returned, but until it is, no rights rest in them and no obligation rests on us.

I do not think
that that transaction would be sustained by any court of law in the world. I do not believe it would be held that the Grand Trunk directors or a majority of the shareholders
1430 '

could legally take any action by which the stock of the minority might be confiscated. The people who hold that stock have certain rights. The stock may not be worth anything, but it belongs to theim. In some cases it is in the hands of shareholders in countries in Europe. Will this Government confiscate it without paying anything for it? I can well understand that the Grand Trunk Company can control the guaranteed stock, because the people who hold it expect to get bonds of the Dominion of Canada in exchange for it. But I am referring to the stock for which the holders will get nothing. They may expect something and, when the arbitration is over, may find their stock is not worth five cents. They may not ibe willing to surrender it to the company or the Government, tout the minister wishes ns to understand that the Government is going to confiscate stocks in the hands of Dutch holders, for instance, and annihilate their rights. Is that the, position? .

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am very glad to hear the sentiments in general that animate the hon. gentleman. I thoroughly agree with him that it would toe entirely wrong on the part of this Parliament to pass a law which would confiscate the property of any person simply because we, or, indeed, some institution or commission appointed toy us, declared that the stock was of no value. Such a course would toe arbitrary, highhanded and wholly indefensible. I commend that sentiment to the hon. gentleman's consideration, particularly in reference to the Canadian Northern stock, and I am sorry that it did not occur to him at the time of the discussion in connection with that subject. In relation to this we do not presume to do anything of the sort. We first of all ask that the Grand Trunk Company, toy its shareholders, take such action as legally binds all the shareholders in this regard. Until the company takes that action we can neither assert nor enjoy any rights under the agreement. They must so ratify the agreement that it will have a legal effect, binding their shareholders to comply therewith. That done, then there can be no confiscation on our part.
Can legal authority be given for such action?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They must have legal authority to take that action. We must be advised on the highest legal authority that the action is, competent on their part.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am sure the Grand Trunk people would not undertake to do it unless they knew there was legal authority.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister says that the agreement will provide for ratification of it by the shareholders. Why should the agreement not also provide that this Parliament should ratify it?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is what this Parliament is engaged on now.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Parliament
does not know the terms o-f the agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We authorize the entering into of the agreement on the terms set out in the Bill. Parliament is now engaged in doing what the shareholders will afterwards be asked to do.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The shareholders of the Grand Trunk will be given the privilege of knowing the terms they are called upon to ratify, but this Parliament is being asked to authorize an agreement, the terms of which it does not know. I would ask the minister if at is fair to the people of Canada, that their own representatives should be asked to give their consent to an agreement the terms of which they do not know, and which will not become binding until the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, who are the other party to the agreement, ratify. It is putting Parliament in a most extraordinary position. The people have absolutely no rights in this Parliament in accordance with the procedure the minister is adopting. I cannot emphasize too forcibly what I believe every member on this side feels strongly, and what I am sure many members on the other side feel equally strongly, that the Government has no right to ask this Parliament to assent to a transaction involving the expenditure of millions of dollars, not only in one year but for many years, and give Parliament no opportunity to ratify the terms of that agreement, while on the other hand they reserve to the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Company the right of ratification before the agreement goes into effect.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman would have the right to become quite in-

dignant if his facts were anything approaching accuracy. But they are not. The terms of the agreement are set out in the Bill.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Where are they?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In the Bill, tlie clauses of which hon. members will not let us get to the consideration of. We are only at Clause 2. The Bill is an embodiment of the terms of the agreement to be entered into. Nothing can be in the agreement that is in the slightest degree inconsistent with the definite terms set out in the Bill. If there is any term which the hon. member thinks should be in the agreement, or any which he is of opinion should be struck out, he is at liberty to move an amendment to that effect. We cannot do anything that the Bill does not authorize.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Will the minister say what is meant by the following:
/
The said agreement shall contain provisions for the defining of the companies, properties and interests, comprised in the Grand Trunk system, and, including the terms and provisions hereinafter set forth, may contain such other terms and conditions as the parties may agree upon.
What is meant by the words, " such other terms and conditions as the parties may agree upon?" These are the terms and conditions of which nothing whatever is said in this Parliament and of which this Parliament knows nothing.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: These terms and conditions cannot in any way conflict with the terms and conditions, " hereinafter set forth."

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is the meaning of the words I have quoted ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There must be details. It would take a very long time to work out all the details of an agreement of that sort.
We will have a reasonable time to work out all the details of the agreement with the Grand Trunk. The Bill establishes the principle. There is nothing in the world to bind Parliament in that. Parliament is free and untrammelled. There will be details of organization and it is the part of wisdom to allow freedom that these may be taken care of in order that the public interest may be protected. The hon. gentleman talks about this being an invasion of parliamentary rights. I do not doubt for a moment that you could go back to the days of Confederation and trace Bills almost yearly that authorized the Governor in Council to enter
into agreements or to make law by regulation. The principle of our legislation is that the' main lines are laid down in the Bill and the details are worked out by the Governor in Council under the authority of the Bill. Parliament has been doing this not only every year, but almost every week since ^Confederation.
