Everything in the way of authority such as is here sought is sought in almost all legislation that comes before this House.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If the minister Would be agreeable, when we come to the section, to strike out the words " pr upon such other terms and conditions as the parties may agree upon," meaning terms and conditions other than those contained in the Bill, it would meet the objection.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would be agreeable to insert the words " not inconsistent with the terms of this Bill."

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That would be a slight concession.

I would like the minister to tell us what he means by the words " and with such other companies and interests as the Government may think necessary." If we are dealing with the Grand Trunk, what necessity have we to deal with other companies and interests? There seems to be a nigger in the wood-pile. Let the minister tell us the name of these companies and parties interested.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That, I understand, has been fully explained. I have not given any study to it and I may not have it exactly right. Subject to correction-because I am sure the explanation given about it would be correct-I would say that it may be found necessary that the Government should get the assent of certain subsidiary companies to certain provisions of the Bill. It might be, for example, that the Grand Trunk might not have the right to the assignment of certain rights in respect to a subsidiary company. They might have a lease of a railway, but they might have no right to assign that lease. I do not see what restraint there might be, upon them. The illustration I have suggested would seem to me to be a very unlikely one. I would presume that if, as a matter of extra precaution, we found it necessary to take some action in respect to some concession or subsidiary company we could do so.

It would be interesting to find cut all about these leases. If we are going to~ deal with the Grand Trunk

let us deal with the Grand Trunk, and let us not bay, or deal on the side with, subsidiary companies of any kind.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not think it is
at all probable that there is any lease; in fact, I do not think that what I suggested is very likely to occur for the reason that the Grand Trunk Company will be the Grand Trunk Company after we get the Stock just the same as it was before and any rights it had will be just the same and not one whit less. But it may be that in the public interest some further concession should be secured from one of the subsidiary companies, possibly from the Grand Trunk Pacific. This will enable us to do it if it is considered necessary. 1 presume the draughtsman of the legislation thought it wise to put that in. I did not make a special inquiry on that point myself, but in view of the fact that the explanation is already on Hansard, given at a previous time. I think it should satisfy the hon. gentleman.	.

Are we to understand
' that the companies and interests mentioned are companies and interests which may be created for the purpose of dealing with the Government in acquiring these rights of subsidiary companies? Or are they actually existing companies holding these rights at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They actually hold them now.
Mr. DECHENE. Will the minister give the names of these companies?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They are all here on
pages 39 and 40.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Does the
company own any property in Europe or Asia?	"

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not that I know of.

They have very fine
offices in London which will go to the Government, I presume.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If England is considered as being in Europe I would presume that they would. But they have no property on the mainland of Europe or Asia that I am aware of.
At what does the minister place the total liabilities of the lines to be taken over which now operate on American soil?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is given on page 40.

Do I understand that
these roads, a last of which is given in this blue-book, are to he taken over when - we take over the Grand Trunk and Grand Trunk -Pacific?	,

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We had the right to
take them over because we will have a controlling interest in them.
M,r. DEVLIN:	The minister could not
tell me what are the real lines to be taken over? The (Minister of Railways said before the minister (Mr. Meighen) came in this evening that we would take over the branch -lines.
Mr. M1EIGHEN: It is incorrect, strictly speaking, to -talk about our taking over -the branch lines. We take over the s-tock of the Grand Trunk; that is ail we take over. In taking over that, we take over all the rights of the company. One of the rights of the company is to abandon any property in respect to which it has no obligation except -the .ownership of its -stock.

The -minister knows perfectly well -that I am not asking for a -repetition of the statement on that aspect of the matter. The statement was made before -the minister came in by the Minister of Railways that we were going to take over subsidiary lines. He -said- there is no doubt about it. I am -simply -asking if these lines are some of the subsidiary lines the -Government has already got or means to take over?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The (Minister of Railways, not being -a lawyer, does not see the full significance of the 'hon. gen-tle-m-an's words. The Minister of Railways does not mean that we are to take over the roads in the sense the hon. gentleman has in mind at all. He simply means we -take over the main company with all the rights of the .main company. One of the rights that we secure is to take over such subsidiary companies as the parent company h.as the right to operate. It is our intention, in so far as they are assets to take them a,11 over, but I assure the hon. gentleman if there is any American company for example, in which, in so far - as operation i-s concerned, only the people over there are interested and which is more of a liability than an asset, we will not be bothered with it.

I do not exactly gather the meaning of the minister's statement, but I assume that in the case of some of those
[Mr. Dech&ne.l

roads which are on American soil, notwithstanding their heavy liabilities, if the Government finds them profitable to take over they will do so.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have no taking over to do. We will operate them. If the roads are profitable we will operate them just the same as they are operated now.
Then they will be operated, not for the benefit of the people of this country but for the benefit of the people over there?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, they will be operated for our benefit in the event of their being profitable. That was the condition expressed by the hon. gentleman.
If they are profitable?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If they are profitable, do we not get the profit? Why then should we throw that profit away?

I am not speaking about their being profitable at the present moment. History tells us, and best information we get shows that they have not been profitable. The minister now reasons that if these railways are profitable they have a right to take them over.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Operate them.

If I understand correctly, one of the reasons that might make them profitable for the people of this country is to get the advantage of the ports of Portland, Boston and New London. Is that right or is it wrong?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not think it is very right, but the hon. gentleman knows just as much about it as any one knows. It may be profitable to operate a road in the United States; if it is not profitable, if it is not of advantage in this country to operate the road, we are not going to do it, the hon. gentleman can be sure of that. We are not concerned in building up American ports for American roads, we have tried to let the hon. gentleman understand that for many years gone by. But it might be of value to run a road as a feeder. It might be such an integral part of the system that though there might be a deficit in respect to the books of that company itself, still its resultant benefit to the system might be such that it would be to our advantage as a Canadian people that the Grand Trunk should operate that road. That is the principle that we will be guided by.

I presume that is the only information in a concrete form that we can
get. I will therefore have to declare myself satisfied.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: One clause in this Bill provides that three arbitrators are to be appointed, and according to the wording of that clause the agreement would contain the name of the arbitrators. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We are not at that clause yet.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am simply asking for information.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: To which clause does the hon. gentleman refer?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I think clause
6 is the one that refers to the appointment of arbitrators. The point I wish 'to ask the minister about is this: As I read the Bill referring to the question we were speaking of a moment ago as to the knowledge the respective parties would have, the shareholders would know the names of the arbitrators before they are asked to ratify this measure.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The agreement will not contain the names of the arbitrators. The appointment of arbitrators, is covered in a letter of October 9th addressed by myself to Sir Alfred Smithers; the point is more fully stated there than it is in the Bill The terms of that letter 12 midnight, will be strictly followed. It says the agreement shall provide that each side shall name an arbitrator and that the two so appointed shall name a third, or, failing an agreement on the part of these two, the third arbitrator shall be named by Sir Walter Cassels and Sir Louis Davies, acting together. That is what the agreement provides.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: Before the clause passes, we want some more information from the minister as to the correctness of the statements in the blue book. At page 45 the capital stock of the Atlantic and St. Lawrence railway, guaranteed or preferred, is given as $5,483,800 at six per cent; on .page 51 speaking of the same company reference is made to "five per cent on capital stock of $5,484,000 as rental". The minister will notice that makes considerable difference on the annual contribution of this 200 odd miles of railway. Perhaps he can explain which of these statements is right.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The capital stock of the Atlantic and St. Lawrence railroad is shown
1434.

on page 40 as $5,484,800 and noted at six per cent.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
Now if the minister will
turn to page 51 he will notice the capitalization given somewhat differently, and at five per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The statement put on Hansard to-day gives the figures exactly the same as at page 40, at six per cent.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: So the statement given at page 51 is not a correct statement?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That does not necessarily follow, because the statement at page 51 shows the condition as at December 31, 1917. It may be-I have not looked into it -that the stock matured and that the interest rate was raised. That is possible, but it does not follow that there is any error.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
The minister cannot get
away with that explanation, because on page 40 the date is exactly the same, December 31, 1917.
Carried.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: No, it is not carried. This involves $60,000 a year and we want to know something about it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Well, six per cent is
evidently right. On page 40 the capitalization is of December 31, 1917. It may be that the capitalization figures are as of that date and the interest was put in as it stands now. It may possibly be a misprint, it may possiby be an error, but the correct information is given in the statement placed in Hansard to-day which agrees with the statement on page 40 that it is six per cent interest. It is by way of rental.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
Your information on page
51 is not right. It may or may not be a misprint, but that it is not right, the minister will admit.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would not like to say it is not right, although it is possible it is not right.

There is discrepancy in the mileage that I would like to get an explanation of. At page 26 the mileage of the Grand Trunk in the United States is placed at 1,665, and on page 33 the mileage in operation in the United States is given as 1,367.5 miles. V/hich of these is correct, because it makes a difference of 297 miles?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman
will look at the top it says that the total

mileage operated in United States owned or controlled by the Grand Trunk is 1,367.5 miles. In the next column the mileage operated in the United States under the heading of "Leased or Rights'' is given, 298.0, and the total is 1,665.5, exactly as set out on page 26.

The Minister of the Interior made reference to a statement giving the guarantees in connection with the Central Vermont Railway Company. I find on page 40 of the blue book in the funded debt an item of $9,521,000 in respect of the Central Vermont Railway Company; this is in the statement of December 31, 1917. With regard to the $30,'000,000 bond issue in respect of the Southern New England railway, has any part of that been issued, and at what rate of interest?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is a four per cent bond issue of the Central Vermont railway. The amount issued is $11,750,000 as set out in the statement which was put on Hansard to-day.
Is the $9,000,000 that is shown on page 40 part of the $11,000,000 referred to in the statement which was put on record to-day?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That $9,000,000 on page 40 is under the heading, "Funded Debt, Bonds and Debentures, Notes-Loans." Then, in the next column, under the heading "To public, equipment, etc.," there is an item of $441,000, and there is a further item of $808,000 under "Held by public, common," making a total held by the public of $10,770,900. That would be a portion of the amount set out in the statement filed to-day.	-
When was that bond issue?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not know the date, but the authorization was on May 4, 1916. Of course, the issue must have been since that. But we are not concerned about the exact date, because there are no arrears of interest.
The minister says that $11,000,000 of bonds have been issued. How much mileage has been constructed with the proceeds of this issue of bonds?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Central Vermont, 246.3 miles.
What part of the Southern New England railway has been constructed with the proceeds of this $11,000,000 worth of bonds?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: None of it.
Although this money has been spent since 1917, there is absolutely no added mileage shown?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Apparently this was
only a charter; none of the bonds were used for the Southern New England road.

What was the nature of the agreement that gave the Central Vermont the right to issue bonds guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company for the purpose of constructing the Southern New England railway?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Central Vermont was authorized to issue $30,000,000 worth of bonds, and out of that, I gather, they had power to build part of the Southern New England railway. As a matter of fact, they did not do it, so it does not matter what the power was. What they have issued of bonds, they have used for their own road. The indebtedness, as has already been given and as embodied in Hansard, is $11,750,000.
All bonds.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
I have said that there is an item of $9,521,000 in the statement as of 31st December, 1917. When was the extra million dollars issued?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot give the date of the issue of the bonds. The interest is paid on them up to date, so what is the difference?
The minister says that if the interest is paid it does not matter how much we spend?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The interest is paid
up to date. We are not concerned in the date of the bond issue; we are concerned with the obligation in respect of the subsidiary companies-that is, so far as we are concerned at all. What difference does it make when the bonds of a subsidiary company were issued? What we want to know is what is against it now, and that we know.
Who paid the interest on these bonds?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Company.

We were told to-day that the Central Vermont Railway Company were indebted to the Grand Trunk for something like $8,000,000, so that the interest could not have been paid by the Central Vermont; if they paid it, they must have borrowed it from the Grand
Trunk. If this company was in a position to pay interest, why did it not pay the Grand Trunk?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It has paid its interest. The Grand Trunk responsibility is set out just above on page 51 as follows:
The Grand Trunk railway guarantee the interest on the bonds by traffic contract up to an amount equal to thirty per cent of the gross receipts from interchange business.
Apparently the Central Vermont owe the Grand Trunk over $8,000,000. What control has the Grand Trunk over the Central Vermont now?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The hon, gentleman will see exactly the control they have if he refers to page 35-72 per cent of the stock.
How are we to collect this $8,000,000 from them?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Draw on them, I suppose.
And they will borrow more from the Grand Trunk to pay it with, is that the idea?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not know where they will borrow it.
Where may the statement be found of the assets of the Central Vermont?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: On page 40, as well as pages 34 and 35.
What is there on page 40 about the assets of this company?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Well, they own 246-3 miles of railway in the United States.
Anything else? Are those all the assets they have? Is there no rolling stock?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, there is rolling stock.
What are the liabilities?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is only three minutes since I gave that. They amount to $11,750,000 as appearing on the statement laid on the Table to-day and put on Hansard.
Does that $11,000,000 include the $8,000,000 which is owing to the Grand Trunk by the Central Vermont, or is that a bond issue as the minister said a few minutes ago?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The blue-book on page 40 shows it as of December 31, 1917.
The minister stated that there were $11,000,000 worth of bonds issued

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: and outstanding against the Central Vermont. Another minister of the Crown told us to-day that the Central Vermont owed the Grand Trunk Railway system) some $8,000,000. I am asking now what are the liabilities of the Central Vermont. Where is the statement of the Central Vermont showing the assets and liabilities?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Central Vermont have a deficit, as shown on page 54.
That is an operating deficit?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Unless i)t appears that we are under an obligation to operate it or that it pays to operate it as a feeder to the .Grand Trunk system, then it may be abandoned. But as I pointed out a while ago to the satisfaction of those who listened, although there may be a deficit on that, that must be made up by a surplus somewhere else before there can be any final surplus in the whole system. The final surplus is shown, and that is what we are interested in. We do not pay the deficit because we get something else.
Where is that shown?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: On the first page of the blue-book after the correspondence.

I question whether the minister will be able to abandon the road, because the Grand Trunk has guaranteed 30 per cent of the gross receipts from interchange of business. I do not think he can say now that he will not operate it at all when he is bound to run it and to pay to the shareholders 30 per cent of the gross receipts.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not think that is right. What the blue-book says is this that (the Grand Trunk guarantees them up to 30 per cent of the gross receipts. That is to say, if the Grand Trunk operates the road, it guarantees up to 30 per cent of the gross receipts from interchange of business. That is apparently an obligation, but it is only to the extent of receipts. Supposing the whole thing is a liability, it must be set off by a corresponding asset which we would gelt for nothing as a result.
The whole thing is a liability so far as the Grand Trunk is concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That may be, but the aggregate shows a surplus to the stockholders of the Grand Trunk, and consequently there must be other assets bringing in revenue which have been set off against this liability.
Is there a surplus of earnings?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is what is shown by the Drayton-Acworth report which the hon. member admires so much.

What does this book
show?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The same thing.

Where are the surplus
assets sufficient ito pay the $2,433,000 that the hon. member is so anxious to vote to some parties unknown?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Page 56.

On page 56 it~appears that no dividends were paid in 1918, nor in 1917 upon this stock. Why does the minister deliberately attempt to mislead the members of this House? I am asking the minister where he finds his revenue to pay interest on this appropriation which he is in such haste to get through this House?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We are in no hurry.
Why does the. minister not furnish the information if he is in no hurry and let us debate it intelligently?
Oh, oh.

I know that will be too much to expect from hon. members opposite. I believe that not one in ten of them have read this statement and that not one in twenty-five would understand it if they read it. Not only are members sitting behind the minister unable to give the information, but the members of the Government themselves are unable to give it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There are some people that some information will never sink into.
On page 45 is shown a surplus of $8,760. Where does the minister get the surplus to set off against the deficit?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman is getting sleepy.

That is no answer at all. The minister says that he is willing to give us the information. If he wants to sit here all night, provided that he will furnish us with information, I am perfectly willing to slay with him. The Minister of Railways furnished some information today. He got the liabilities up to $527,000,000 and finally up to $539,000,000, and surely we are entitled to whatever information the Government may have. There is no reason in the world why they should hide it unless they have some reason which they

have not given to the committee. They are proposing to guarantee $60,000,000 worth of bonds, and on the operation as it stands to-day and for the last two years, a deficit has been shown. There is no possible chance of earning sufficient to pay the interest on these bonds. The question was asked why the Government were in such haste to guarantee them, and no satisfactory answer was given. When the minister says that the information is all in this blue-book, and then turns to page 56 as he did and finds that there was no interest paid on those bonds for the last two years, and when he turns to the [DOT] Drayton-Acworth report which says that no interest should have been paid for the last ten years, I do not see how he can possibly hope to justify his case with any person but his very docile and gentle following who take absolutely no interest in this or other matters before the House since they have found that they are afraid to go home in the dark. There is no use their going home any more. The country will expect this information and the Opposition will expect it, and if my hon. friend is honest with the House he will give it to us. I do not see why he should not at least make an attempt at it.

I have noticed many times that the hon. member (Mr. Cahill) is very much worried about hon. members on this side of the House not taking part in this discussion. I should just like to enlighten him why. The reason they do not, if my conclusion is correct, is that most of the members on this side of the House do not like to get up and take part in this discussion unless they have something to say. My hon. friend does not seem to have any such scruples.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I should like to draw the minister's attention to what seems a little incomplete in the answer he gave a moment ago. Adverting to the right reserved to the shareholders of the Grand Trunk to ratify the agreement entered into, I asked the minister if a similar right was not to be reserved to Parliament. He replied that that right was to a certain extent being reserved in view of the fact that the terms and provisions of the agreement would be made known once this Bill had passed Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I did not say that at all.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What did my hon. friend say?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I said the terms and provisions were set out here, and only details that are ordinarily left to the Governor in Council are authorized by the Bill. Not only are the terms of the Bill set out here but even the details can be provided by Parliament to any extent hon. gentlemen desire. I did not say that publication of the Bill was of any assistance to Parliament.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What the minister has just said does not affect the point one way or the other. What I wish to point out is that all the knowledge this Parliament will have after this Bill is passed will be common knowledge. It will be known to the shareholders of the Grand Trunk just exactly to the same extent as it will be known to the* representatives of the people here, but notwithstanding that fact the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway Company aro to have the additional privilege of ratifying the agreement that has been made after this Act has been passed. The Government is not permitting the representatives of the people in Parliament to have a similar privilege. I wish to ask the minister how he can justify giving a right to the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway Company which he is withholding from the people of this country through their representatives in this Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Because he is not
doing it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: He is doing it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Parliament has. the first opportunity. It deals with the matter first by this Bill fully, and in the way Parliament invariably deals with such matters. Everything is here that Parliament requires. If there is anything Parliament desires to put in the Bill it can put it in.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is it not true that if this Bill passes Parliament and becomes an Act, the Government then draws an agreement between the Grand Trunk and itself?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In accordance with the terms of the Bill.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is correct. The terms of the Bill, once it becomes an Act, will be known equally well to the Grand Trunk shareholders as to the people's representatives in this Parliament., That is true?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Then is it not true that after this has been done and before the agreement becomes binding, it has
I

to 'be ratified by the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway Company?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The agreement is the same as the Bill.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Will the minister answer my question? Is it not true?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Then is it not true also that the ministry is withholding from this Parliament a similar right of ratification?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: But we haven't it now.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If there are any details the hon. gentleman wants to be embodied in the Bill, let him move accordingly.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I must ask
the minister, if possible, to give me a direct answer to a direct question. The agreement which is to be drawn is something which is unknown to this Parliament and will be unknown when this Parliament prorogues. In view of that fact the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway 'Company are going to be preserved in their right of ratifying the agreement before they become bound by it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The agreement, I repeat, is embodied in the Bill.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is true.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Then what more does the hon. gentleman want? If it is embodied in the Bill, is he not considering the agreement when he is considering the Bill?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The essence
of the agreement may be embodied in the Bill, but we have had enough experience with some measures the Government has had to do with to know that the terms that may come out of an agreement which the Government may draft will not perhaps adhere as closely to some of the provisions of the 'Bill as the representatives of the people in Parliament might wish.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman just give me one instance, and the term of the agreement that was not consistent with the Bill?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I shall 'be very glad to give the hon. gentleman numerous instances later on.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Now is the best time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Now is the
time I want to get an answer to the question I am asking.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
made an allegation that we had departed from the authority of an Act and embodied something in an agreement that was not in accordance with the Act. Now is the hon. gentleman's time to make good his allegation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Not on this
Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Just give us an example in connection with any Bill.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: When the hon. gentleman has given me a satisfactory answer to my question. '

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I will guarantee the
hon. gentleman will never be satisfied with my answer.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is'quite correct.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He cannot make good his allegation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not think the country will be satisfied with the minister's answer. At this time, of all times, the ministry has reason to have some little regard for public opinion. A good deal has been said in the House to-day about the battle of the rights of the people. The President of the Privy Council, just before he went out, spoke of the Government looking after the interests of the people in connection with this measure. The people have a chance to express their views on certain questions on different occasions; they have had a chance to-day. Five by-elections have been held and four of them have gone against the ministry.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: How many went against the hon. gentleman?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: - I have said four have gone against the ministry, which I think ought to be a sufficient index of public feeling.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: How many went against the hon. gentleman?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I am not aware that any have. What I wish further to point out is this: That when public opinion is asserting itself against a ministry, as it is against this Government throughout the whole country, it is perfectly evident that the public are aroused against the executive usurping the power of Parliament at every turn. It is time the ministry reconsider their practice of ignoring Parliament altogether. I think the minister would be well advised to let this clause

stand for a time and confer with his colleagues, and see if it is not possible to give the House the assurance that at least the same privileges will be reserved for the people of this country as are being reserved by the Government's legislation to the shareholders of the Grand Trunk.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The same privilege are reserved, as the hon. gentleman well knows, and has been told a dozen times. The agreement is embodied here in the Bill, as he has admitted himself. Being embodied here, we are now considering it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is not embodied here.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
said so himself.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If the minister understood that he misunderstood me. I had no intention of indicating in any shape or form that the agreement was embodied in the Bill. My remarks to him were distinctly addressed with a view to having the terms embodied in the Bill, because otherwise I had no feeling of confidence in the possibility of their being embodied in the agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If they are not embodied here, we cannot make the agreement, because it is only to the extent they are embodied here that we can make it. If we depart in any way from anything set out here, the agreement is invalid. The hon. gentleman did say the agreement was embodied here, but if he wishes to depart from that, all right. He went so far as to allege we had exceeded the authority, granted us by Parliament and had made an agreement not authorized by Parliament. I challenged him to make good his allegation, and I repeat the challenge now. We cannot depart from this Bill. If we do depart from it the agreement is invalid. This is the way universally adopted in almost every piece of legislation. The power of making an agreement in accordance with the terms embodied in a Bill is exercised universally by governments.
It was exercised by the Government he was in every three years he was in it. There is nothing at all inconsistent in that exercise with the principle of the rights of the people, and such an assertion is merely playing to the gallery-if you can dignify it by that description. Let the hon. gentleman make good his allegation that this Government at any time departed from the authority of Parliament in regard to any provision in any Bill.,

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I desire the minister to answer my questions.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is a question that he will have-to answer out of the House if not in it, and it is in the interest of every hon. member as well as of the people that it should be answered satisfactorily. I would ask the minister again: On what ground does he withhold from the people, exercising their rights through representatives in Parliament, the right to ratify this agreement when he gives that same right to the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway Company?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He does not do so. Parliament is exercising the same right now as the shareholders will exercise later on. If the hon. gentleman feels that there is any evidence on the part of the country that it is opposed to the Bill I would like to intimate to him that virtually all the candidates, except himself, elected in the byelections would favour this measure. I must congratulate the hon. gentleman for his optimism if he sees any great encouragement for himself in any recent contest.

The member for Prince has claimed that the procedure of the Government will give the Grand Trunk shareholders a privilege which is not to be given Parliament. Does the Minister of the Interior deny that?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, I deny that.

Then let us follow it point by point. When this Bill passes it will be as well known to the shareholders of the Grand Trunk as it is to us and the public. We stand on even terms to that extent; the Grand Trunk shareholders have certain knowledge, and we have the same. Then an agreement will be drawn up and submitted to the Grand Trunk shareholders, but not to the Parliament of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That will be true if there is anything in the agreement which would be of assistance to Parliament now and which is not in the Bill. There cannot be, and if the hon. gentleman thinks that something should be in the agreement he is at liberty to bring it before Parliament.

The contention of my hon. friend from Prince is that the shareholders of the Grand Trunk will have a privilege in this matter which Parliament will not have, and he is absolutely correct in that contention. The Grand Trunk

shareholders will not be content with this Bill; they will demand the details of the agreement. The minister says that the agreement is not of importance to us but it is all-important to them. If it is true that the agreement must be in the terms of the Bill, that is true for the Grand Trunk as well as for us. But that statement will not satisfy the Grand Trunk shareholders. My hon. friend knows it will not, and therefore he will produce a written agreement in all its details. The Grand Trunk shareholders will insist on seeing the details of the agree-meift and will not be content with any mere statement of the principles of the contract. My hon. friend will give them a detailed agreement and that privilege will be denied Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member must know that time and again shareholders authorize their directors to proceed exactly in this way. This is the common practice with companies and Parliaments. If it is possible to prepare the details in which, as every one knows, Parliament is not interested but which, if it is interested, it can embody in the Bill, it will be all right. But certainly no advantage is being taken of Parliament. The procedure is regular, and nothing is being withheld. If the hon. gentleman has something he would like to see included in the Bill by way of .minutiaj it can come before Parliament. We have everything that we need in the Bill.

.My hon. friend cannot get away from the fact that we shall not have the agreement before us. whereas the Grand Trunk shareholders will. It. does not meet the case of my hon. friend to say that what we have before us involves everything of importance. That will not be enough for the Grand Trunk shareholders, and my hon. friend himself does not ask them to be content with that. This agreement has to be made subject to the approval of the Grand Trunk.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They may approve just as we are approving, by authorization to their directors along these lines.

That will not he the method of procedure. There will be a meeting of the Grand Trunk shareholders and they Will have the agreement before them. I have no fear that they will reject the agreement because it is too good a thing.
Will the agreement hold the Grand Trunk Company liable for their guarantees on the Grand Trunk Pacific?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If they are not liable how will the agreement make them liable?
That is not the question.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Really, the hon. gentleman does not understand the point; that is absolutely proved. Talk about hairsplitting; it is skull-splitting that is necessary 'in this case. The Grand Trunk is under certain obligations. This agreement does not relieve them of those obligations.
I will not add another word for fear of \ confusing the subject in the hon. gentleman's mind.

Or in your own mind. Now, in regard to the $15,000,000, the members on this side asked the Minister of Railways if the Government intended to hold the Grand Trunk liable for that amount and he said they would. What is the answer to that question? Will the agreement provide that the $15,000,000 shall be taken into account by the arbitrators?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has given the answer himself and he wants to know what the answer is.' He said he was answered that they would be held liable.
My hon. friend can make himself appear sillier than any one else.
Oh, oh.
Burlesque.

Will you provide that the arbitrators shall hold the Grand Trunk Company for the guarantee on the Grand Trunk Pacific, and liable for the $15,000,000 loaned from the Dominion of Canada. That is a plain question, and the minister can surely understand it.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The $15,000,000 is a
liability against the Grand Trunk, and the arbitrators, when considering the award, must take it, as well as any other liability, into consideration.
Mr. .T. H. SINCLAIR: We are proposing to submit the value of the common stock and preference stock to arbitration, and nothing more. The question was raised a few days ago as to why we should not make it more definite and submit other questions such as guarantees and debts owing in respect to the Grand Trunk Pacific. The minister said at that time that it would all be provided for in the agreement. Now, we are told that the agreement is exactly the same as the Bill. But if the agreement is to be definite and to provide for these things should not Parliament see it so as to judge whether or not everything is included in it?

Mr.- MEIGHEN:	By Ihe provisions of
the agreement, as embodied in the Bill, all these things must be taken into consideration. How can you value stock until you take into account the liabilities of the company that issued it? The provisions embodied in the Bill we are now considering provide that all these things must be taken into consideration.

I do not wish to delay the committee, but I must return for a moment to the contention of the Leader of the Opposition, that the Grand Trunk shareholders will be given a privilege and right which will not be given to the people of Canada through their representatives. The minister said that we are now exercising that right, because all the things essential to the agreement are set forth in this Bill. My answer was that the Grand Trunk people would not be satisfied with a general statement but would demand the details of the agreement. My hon. friend brings in the argument- he had to do it-that the Grand Trunk people may do just the same as we are doing now; they may not have a meeting at all. But if my hon. friend will turn to section 7 he will read as follows:
As soon as said agreement has been ratified by a majority of the holders of the stocks enumerated in the preamble to this Act, present in person or by proxy and voting at a special general meeting of such stockholders duly called for the purpose of considering such agreement.
You propose that they are to have all the details of the agreement and that the representatives of the people of Canada are not to have them.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: But they can authorize them to enter into an agreement without specifying the terms.
Not under this Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Bill provides that the agreement shall be entered into before it is submitted to them. But even then they can do it by authorizing the directors to act.
But they have to meet for this purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I see.
But our Parliament will not -meet for this purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The agreement will be known to the shareholders just a,s soon as they have dealt with the matter. But the hon. gentleman knows that there is nothing
in the whole thing because we have every opportunity to do anything and everything that they can do themselves. There is nothing in the world that Parliament need not consider to the minutest detail. If the hon. gentleman desires to keep on discussing until the agreement can be prepared, we are doing the -best we can.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: We will wait.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The agreement is 'being worked out. I do not know how long it is going to take.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I think hon. gentlemen on this side of the House would all prefer to wait. We would like the Government to bring the agreement down before this House prorogues.
Mr. ROBiB: In view of the statement made by the minister who is the legal sponsor for this Bill in the House, would it not be better for the' Minister of Railways or his representatives to sit down with the officials of the Grand Trunk and put a valuation om this property? They could do it much better than three arbitrators whom we do not know. Then, let them come before Parliament with the whole proposition and let the people know what it will cost. Let us put through whatever temperance legislation or prohibition measures are required, and which the minister has brought before Parliament, and then adjourn-not prorogue-for a month so that the Government may come before the House with a clear cut pro-position.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There will be no adjournment for a month. We are getting along as fast as we can with the agreement. We have offered hon. gentlemen all the time they wanted. If they want to keep on discussing this until the agreement is ready, we are just as ready as they are. It is simply a burlesque, simply a waste of the time and money of this country. Hon. gentlemen know it and the people know it. They know the agreement is embodied in this Bill. I think they all know that and if they do not know it let them put it in. All this talk is mere humbug.

The minister first stated that he would give us all the time necessary for debate but some of his followers seem to be getting excited and nervous. The Minister of Railways stated that the Grand Trunk's liabilities to the Grand Trunk Pacific would he taken into account. I would like to ask him what is meant by the statement on page 8, clause 1 :



The Government to take over the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway and branch lines and the Grand Trunk Railway Company; to acquire all assets, and to assume all obligations of both companies.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It means take them over subject to their obligations.
Taking over one subject to the obligation of the other? You are taking them over subject to the Grand Trunk's obligations?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific obligations. I gave the hon. gentleman a statement this afternoon of the obligations of the Grand Trunk to the Grand Trunk Pacific.

When the Minister of the Interior first introduced this Bill before the House he stated that the Government were going to hold the Grand Trunk to the Grand Trunk Pacific guarantee. I asked him how much he considered that guarantee to involve, if he would consider $30,000,000 and settle the obligations of the Grand Trunk in that undertaking. He said " no," that	he would not	accept
$30,000,000 and settle it. In this statement he claims that it will relieve the Grand Trunk of their obligation to the Grand Trunk Pacific. I would like to know if we are to take the minister's statement as accurate when he says we are going to hold them to the Grand Trunk Pacific obligation, or his statement accurate when he says we are not going to hold them to their Grand Trunk Pacific obligation?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I have answered that question a dozen times and I have said that the Grand Trunk obligations should be taken into consideration by the arbitrators. There has never been any member of the Government who has said they would not be taken into consideration and it is hardly fair-
Turn to page 8. .

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I want to settle that question.
Settle it by reading your official report.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
(reading)
The Government to take over the Grand Trunk Pacific railway and branch lines and the Grand Trunk Railway Company; to acquire all assets, and to ^assume all obligations of both companies.
That is all right. That is what I have stated. The arbitrators will value the

stock. All that, will be taken into consideration. The Government has assumed all these liabilities and when they assume them they are to value the stock of the Grand Trunk. The Drayton-Acworth report explained that. After considering all these liabilities and Grand Trunk Pacific guarantees, the authors of the Drayton-Acworth report recommend giving a certain amount up to $3,600,000, the Government to assume the liabilities. It is stated in the letter written to Mr. Smithers that the arbitrators must consider the Grand Trunk Pacific liability as a liability against the Grand Trunk when they are valuing the assets.
Will it be embodied in the agreement that they must consider these liabilities?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Of course the agreement will embody the fact that they must consider all the liabilities not only of the Grand Trunk Pacific, which is a subsidiary of the Grand Trunk, but all the liabilities of any other subsidiary company. The Grand Trunk Pacific is a subsidiary company of the Grand Trunk because the Grand Trunk owns the stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Central Vermont and of the long list of other companies that I have named. We must consider the liabilities and assets of every one of these subsidiary companies.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I shall answer the minister's question, although he did not give to my question the answer, in point of directness, which he should have done. He asked me whether, in not submitting this agreement to Parliament, we had reason to feel lack of confidence in the Government's action. I wish to say that Parliament at the time it passed the Act providing for the acquisition by His Majesty of the capital stock of the Canadian Northern, which was assented to on the 20th September, 1917, left the matter of the agreement in the hands of the Government. With what result? With the result that Parliament, having no opportunity to pass upon the terms provided for in the agreement, had no say as to the manner in which the arbitrators should arrive at the valuation, and as a consequence the country lost some $10,000,000 which might have been saved if Parliament had had the opportunity of passing upon that agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has alleged, without attempting to make good the allegation, that Parliament authorized the Government to do something which they departed from in the performance of. The

authority given the Government by the Canadian Northern Railway Act was abided by to the letter in every detail. The hon. gentleman goes over the old harangue that the Government did this, that and the other thing in order, I suppose, to draw a herring across the trail. Let him show wherein, in the body of the agreement with the Canadian Northern shareholders, there is a single clause or a single sentence that in any way departed from the authority granted by Parliament. Then, and not until then, he may make his allegation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I still maintain the hon. gentleman knows very well that unless Parliament has an opportunity of passing upon that agreement

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is not the point at all.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is the point, and the only point I am raising at the moment: That by this Government denying Parliament this right to pass upon this agreement we have no guarantee whatever that something of the same nature may not occur again.

I find on page 51 a number of issues of stock and bonds and referring to the Grand Trunk Western Railway, the statement is made, " which leaves $922,800 worth in the hands of the public." Now, the amount in the hands of the public, according to a statement at page 40 is $11,972,000.
Sbme hon. MEMBERS: Carried.

Are we to drop this
$11,000,000 or will hon. members know what has become of it and where it is? How does this discrepancy occur? What is the explanation of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:

I submit to hon. gentlemen that we have endeavoured to give all the information possible, and have succeeded in that effort very welll. If they will let this clause pass and allow us to go home we will try to furnish any further information which may be desired.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: With reference to what the .minister has just said about passing this clause, the Minister of the Interior intimated that there was a possibility of the agreement being brought down to Parliament before we are through with this measure. If we can get >an .assurance from the Government at the present time-that the agreement will come down in the-course of this debate, I see no reason why this clause should, not pass; but if we have no assurance as to the possibility of the' agreement being brought down, I think we ought to seek all the details we can possibly get.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman can get no assurance from me as to when it will be possible to get that agreement down. We are not delaying it; our instructions are to get on with it. We desire the legislation to pass, otherwise the agreement is not of very much advantage. We will get along with the agreement just as fast as possible. If the agreement can be got ready before we are through with this debate, well and good; then it can be made known. We will certainly not withhold it, but we are certainly not going to delay this debate. We are going to get on with it, giving hon. gentlemen all the time that is necessary for discussion. We promised that from the beginning, and we promised to give all the information desired. Beyond that, no commitment can be made.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Will it be a day or two days, a week or two weeks, a month or two months, before the agreement is brought down?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot give any idea.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister cannot give us that information?
The minister said the instructions to the Government were to get on with the agreement. Of whom was the minister speaking when he said that?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I said the Government's instructions were to get on with the agreement as rapidly as possible.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Will the minister consider going on with other legislation in the meantime pending the submission of the agreement?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not at all.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Then the minister has no intention whatever to bring the agreement down?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not until it is ready.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Has the minister any expectation when the agreement will be ready? Will it be in the course of another fortnight?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot give any estimate at all.
Will the minister tell us what this Grand Trunk junction road is? Where is this road situated?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
It is a subsidiary company of the Grand Trunk Railway system; whether it is in Quebec or Ontario is immaterial. The question is simply asked for the purpose of delay.	.
Some lion. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.

No.
-Mr. J. D. REID: The hon. member knows that it makes no difference where this railway is. The system comprises so many miles of railway, and this line is part of the system. I am prepared to give all the information that is required and that is necessary, but if the hon. gentlemen wish to stay here and ask absurd questions why, I suppose we must stay.

I do not think I have
bothered the minister very much with questions. Here is a road which he states is a subsidiary of the Grand Trunk; yet it does not appear ' in the list of subsidiary companies given in the blue-book. speechtext:
The information may
be found in the French edition at page 34, No. 6-sixty miles of railway, between West Detroit and Fort Gratiot, Michigan. I am sure that it is worth the time of the country when we can save the hon. gentleman the trouble of looking the information up himself.

speechtext:

[Mr. Meiehen.l

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I leave it entirely to
the leader of the Opposition; if he wishes, not to let the clause go through, I will move that the committee rise.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
We have no
such desire on this side; we are quite sincere when we say that all we are after is information.	^

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I shall not ask that this Bill go through without giving my hon. friend all the information that I can. I say, too, that the hour is late and I do not want to hold the Committee; nor do I wish to force through any clause of the Bill. I repeat that we should allow at least one of the twelve clauses of the Bill to pass, but if the leader of the Opposition will not let this clause go through or does not wish it to pass we will report progress. '

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Far from any desire not to make progress, my whole purpose in rising was to get from the minister the assurance that if this clause is permitted to pass we shall not be prejudiced in the matter of getting such information as we may desire to obtain when subsequent clauses are under consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The leader of the Opposition and ahy hon. members on that side will get all the information they want and get it as fast as I can give it to them-that is, if it is at- all possible for me to give it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
In view of that assurance, I have no hesitation in saying that we on this side are quite prepared to let this clause pass.
